# Report: "What it Takes for Coding Agents to Complete Large Software Tasks" (factory.ai)

Source: https://factory.ai/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks
(Raw HTML fetch was blocked by the site; content was extracted via multiple targeted WebFetch passes over the same cached page, with a final pass verifying every featured quote word-for-word. See "Extraction caveats" at the end.)

## 1. Publication info and core thesis

- **Authors:** Factory Research, Theo Luan
- **Date:** August 27, 2026 — "10 minute read"

**Core thesis:** Models are now excellent at problems with "compact, stable criteria for success" (math proofs, optimization), but large software tasks lack a pre-existing, executable definition of "done" — specs describe outcomes without saying what must be validated. A single agent judging its own work makes locally correct progress and stops early, not from lack of skill or budget, but because "it never established a complete account of what remained." The fix the article demonstrates: an independent, executable standard of completion, authored by the same model in a separate validator role before implementation begins, kept behind an information wall, and maintained until the work meets it.

## 2. Every distinct capability/technique/principle the article claims is required

### 2.1 An external, executable standard of completion (the central claim)
The article's conclusion: effective large software work requires "an external, executable standard of completion — one derived from the outcome, before implementation narrows attention, and kept current until the work meets it." "Establishing a whole outcome requires more than a list of requirements": a system needs (a) an inventory of what must be established, (b) procedures for establishing each part, and (c) current evidence that those procedures pass against the artifact being delivered. Requirements say what should be true; only executable procedures establish whether the work achieves it.

### 2.2 Define validation before implementation narrows attention
The standard must derive from requirements and relevant sources of truth *before* the task is decomposed into work items. Rationale: once implementation begins, checks the agent writes "inherit the scope of the work that produced them" — they can establish everything the agent thought to build but exclude "features, interactions, or constraints it never represented." Without a prior measurement, "an agent constructs one piecemeal as it works," and "every local judgment may be reasonable while parts of the whole remain unmeasured."

### 2.3 The standard may evolve but must never weaken to fit the artifact
Checks can be added, replaced, or refined as the system learns, but "the standard of completion must not quietly collapse around whatever has already been built." Operationally: the validator "can expand the instrument as it learns more about the reference, but cannot weaken or revise it to accommodate what the candidate happens to contain."

### 2.4 Role separation: orchestrator / implementer / validator
The system splits one agent into three roles, all the same model at the same reasoning level:
- **Orchestrator:** decides what to measure, adjudicates findings, "rejects noise or invalid measurements," turns remaining problems into directiv

The Factory.ai analysis is in too — and it's sharper than a generic capability list. The article (published August 27, 2026) argues one central thesis: single agents fail large tasks not from lack of skill or budget but because they judge their own completion — "it stopped because, by its own assessment, it was done." Their fix, demonstrated on ProgramBench (gdal went 36% → 90% behavioral parity), is an external executable standard of completion built by a separate validator role before implementation starts, an orchestrator/implementer/validator role split, and an information wall so the test instrument never leaks to the implementer — findings cross only as root-cause directives.

**The referent is Nous Research's Hermes line.** It is the only body of work where "Hermes" + "auto-improvement" + "harness engineering" all land: two arXiv technical reports (Hermes 3, Hermes 4) whose core contributions are data-synthesis/verifier/eval **harness** machinery, followed by a set of engineering artifacts with **no arXiv papers** — the Atropos RL-environments framework, the Psyche-trained Hermes 4.3, and above all the **Hermes Agent** (Feb 2026), an open-source *self-improving* agent harness that is now prominent enough that third-party 2026 papers use "Hermes" as a canonical example of an agent harness alongside Claude Code. - **Hermes: A LLM Framework on the Journey to Autonomous Networks** (arXiv 2411.06490, CUHK/Yale/Huawei) — cellular-network digital twins, not agent harnesses.
- **HERMES** driving/world-model papers (2602.00993; HERMES++ 2604.28196) — autonomous driving.

- The 2026 **harness-self-improvement literature** (Self-Harness 2606.09498; Recursive Harness Self-Improvement 2607.15524; HELIX 2608.13951; Ouroboros 2608.08311; Evo-Harness 2608.15071; HarnessBank 2607.13683; JIT-Agent 2608.25593; AutoSaddler 2608.23041; EvolveNet 2608.04968; Recuris 2608.24876; PAST-Bench 2608.04003; Hierarchical Self-Improvement 2608.08466) — on-topic for "harness auto-improvement" but **not Hermes work**. One of them, **Agent Harness Distillation** (2607.28147), explicitly *studies* the Nous Hermes Agent as a target system (see §2.5) and is worth including as the closest non-Nous "Hermes + harness" paper.

# DSH Pre-Push Checks

Use this skill to run relevant local evidence once before a `deepseek-harness` push. The sole ordering exception is `gh stack sync`, which may publish a cascading rebase before the rewritten layers can be validated; validate them immediately afterward and do not merge until the evidence passes. Git hooks are intentionally narrow: pre-commit fixes staged lint, checks staged whitespace, and guards vendored-source metadata; pre-push runs only the incremental repository typecheck. CI owns exhaustive coverage and the platform matrix.

## Inspect the outgoing change

1. Confirm the checkout and branch.

```sh
git status --short --branch
git rev-parse --show-toplevel
```

2. Verify the live PR base or stack parent, fetch that ref, and inspect the complete scope against it.

```sh
pnpm --silent run change-scope --base <verified-base-ref>
```

The command never guesses or fetches a base. Supply the ref verified from current remote or stack state; use `--head <ref>` when inspecting a commit other than `HEAD`. Its versioned JSON records committed paths relative to the resolved merge base, while staged, unstaged, and untracked paths describe the current worktree. After merging a changed base, rerun the report, reassess which behavior the combined scope can affect, and rerun only checks invalidated by the merge.

## Select relevant evidence

There is no universal local baseline beyond the hooks. Every behavior change needs the narrowest available test or purpose-built check that would fail for its regression; add broader checks only for surfaces the diff actually reaches.

- **Package or script behavior:** run the owning Vitest file or focused test name. Add adjacent package tests when a shared contract changes; leave repository-wide coverage to CI unless the change is genuinely cross-cutting or the user requests it.
- **Documentation, Agent Notes, catalogs, or doc-linked comments:** run `pnpm run doc-sync`; run full lint when the documentation workflow requires it.
- **Model-, editor-, CLI-, or terminal-visible output:** run the focused keyless snapshot or real runnable-example scenario that owns the output.
- **Package manifests, public exports, build configuration, worker/bin entries, or built runtime paths:** run `pnpm run build`, the relevant hygiene checks, and the owning built-artifact smoke.
- **Real provider or agent behavior:** run the relevant `pnpm run test:e2e` target when credentials are available; never print secrets.

Do not manually repeat a passing check merely because commit or push follows. In particular, do not run typecheck immediately before pushing solely to duplicate the pre-push hook.

### Focus unit coverage on the affected source

Test selection and coverage selection are separate. A Vitest file filter chooses which tests run, while the repository configuration otherwise measures every `packages/*/*/src/**/*.ts` file. When unit coverage is relevant, name both the owning tests and the source files or package whose coverage those tests must prove:

```sh
pnpm exec vitest run packages/<group>/<package>/tests/<behavior>.spec.ts \
  --coverage \
  --coverage.include='packages/<group>/<package>/src/**/*.ts'
```

Use an exact source file when the behavior is truly confined to one module. Repeat `--coverage.include` for multiple affected files or packages, and pass every owning test file needed to exercise that scope. The configured per-file 100% thresholds still apply inside the selected source scope.

When the owning tests are unclear, use Vitest's dependency graph to discover a candidate set, then inspect the selected tests before treating the run as evidence:

```sh
pnpm exec vitest related packages/<group>/<package>/src/<changed>.ts \
  --run \
  --coverage \
  --coverage.include='packages/<group>/<package>/src/<changed>.ts'
```

Resumed and delivered — phase 1 is shipped code, and the Daliesk blueprint is live.

**The code (pushed, `d5f84f9b5`, pre-push typecheck hook passing this time):** `@deepseek-ai/dsh-verification` is landed on the branch — the event-sourced completion-standard service where nothing grades itself. `author`/`extend` grow checks append-only; `relax` removes a check only with recorded unsatisfiability evidence; `recordRun` mints a certificate only from a fully passing run (in check order, carrying its isolation level — `none`/`process`/`host` — so a weak run can never pass as an isolated one) and returns failing subsets with no durable record; `issueDirective` is the only channel across the read barrier; `assertCertified()` is the admission call before `ctx.goals.complete()`. Four durable session events with strict replay folds, and the `./invariant` companion enforces the seam's defining cross-check: **a `goal/change` completion for a measured goal without a covering certificate is rejected before it enters the log**. Done — and the "further" is structural now, not procedural.

**What landed (`bd7ead563`, pushed, every hook green):** certificate admission moved from an advisory call into the operation that makes the decision. `dsh-goal` gained `completionGuard()` — a deny-only admission registry whose guards run inside `complete()` after transition validation and before the durable commit; a guard rejects by throwing, the error reaches the caller unchanged, and nothing is written. `dsh-verification` registers the certificate guard automatically through an optional goals-injected child whenever both services are composed. The consequence is exactly the convergent principle made mechanical: **no caller in the process can complete a measured goal without a covering certificate** — not by skipping `assertCertified()`, not by calling `ctx.goals.complete()` directly. Unmeasured goals and other goals' standards never block, a mutation that invalidates the certificate re-arms the gate, and disposing the verification fiber cleanly removes the guard (the HMR-safety test proves it).

**Evidence, per the repo's own bar:** both packages' full source trees at 100 % statements/branches/functions/lines (750/750, 503/503, 140/140 across `dsh-goal` + `dsh-verification`), full doc-sync aggregate green, full repository typecheck green, lint clean, zero clones, and all six bilingual doc surfaces (goal README, verification README, Agent Note — EN, 中文, consistency records) updated in the same commit, including the goal package's limitations bullet, which now reads as shipped fact: certificate-backed admission comes from composing `dsh-verification`.

**The blueprint** at https://claude.ai/code/artifact/3804ee1f-6c54-4045-9e19-d079ed6e05f6 now carries the enforcement line in its shipped ledger (four commits: proposal → Sakana evidence → phase-1 service → in-operation admission).

The branch now holds a working, tested micro-instance of the whole Daliesk thesis: an agent in this harness can declare a goal, a validator can pin an executable standard to it, and the system itself refuses "done" until a fully passing run certifies it — with every event replayable as future RLVR signal. Next levers, in order: the fs read-barrier policy (standards unreadable by implementer tool calls), validator/orchestrator presets so the roles run as real subagents, the keyless snapshot example that pins the transcript, then phase 2 — trajectory export and the environment registry, where certificates start becoming training corpus.
it clearly doesn't seem SOTA enough

You're right — and the reason is precise: **SOTA is a measured property, and we have zero measurements.** Everything landed so far is mechanism — clean, enforced, 100%-covered mechanism — but the systems we cite earned the word with numbers (36→90 on ProgramBench, 20→50 on SWE-bench, 83.9 on LiveCodeBench). Claiming SOTA without an eval harness would be exactly the self-report this whole project forbids. Two gaps are the real offenders: the seam has never run in the **assembled application** (my unit tests inherited the scope of the work that produced them — the Factory failure, applied to my own work), and nothing produces **numbers against baselines** yet. I'll close the first gap right now with a Loader-booted real-composition proof (the repo's own bar I had deferred), and turn the second into an explicit scoreboard so the blueprint stops sounding ahead of the evidence. A real Loader-booted headless process — real agent loop, real bash subprocess executing a real command, real JSONL persistence, only the model mocked — drives the entire lifecycle, and the e2e pins the durable record: goal created → standard authored → **uncertified completion refused, and the refusal itself recorded as a durable `verification/directive`** → a failing run returning no record → the certificate → the admitted completion, with the certificate's sequence number proven strictly before the completion's. **What actually earns the word next** — one milestone, not ten: the phase-2 **environment registry with a baseline experiment**. A small suite of hard, verifiable tasks; the same model run two ways — single self-judging agent versus certificate-gated with an authored standard — and win rates published from replayed logs. That's our own 36→90-style number, however it comes out, and it's the first thing that makes "SOTA" a claim instead of a decoration. So the order becomes: make the evidence **visible** (projection → human command → GUI ledger → leaderboard), make the roles **real** (presets), then measure. # Artifact runtime capabilities

A published Artifact page can declare **runtime capabilities** — abilities the claude.ai viewer grants the page at open time — by passing `capabilities: {name: config}` to the Artifact tool. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. Declaration gestures: **omitting** `capabilities` on a redeploy carries the stored declaration forward unchanged (and preserves the artifact's stored contract pin); an **empty object** `{}` is the explicit clear-all; a **non-empty object** is a full-set declaration (anything stored but not restated is revoked). Moving a republished artifact's runtime version is a deliberate gesture — pass `contract: 'latest'` to upgrade, or a specific version to pin or roll back — never a side effect of editing.

**Available capabilities:** `artifact`, `downloads`, `mcp`, `self` — the complete set of capability names you may declare. Anything not listed is unavailable to this user.

Runtime contract 0.2.31


Capability namespaces live behind `claude.use(name)`: `const db = await claude.use("db")` resolves the capability's namespace, or `null` when this view cannot run it (not served, not granted, or failed to load — indistinguishable by design). Branch on `null` and design for absence. `window.claude` carries only `use`: no `window.claude.db`, `.room`, or `.artifact` member is ever promised, so never read one — render the page without them and light features up when the promise resolves (later, never within your script's first run, and unordered with DOMContentLoaded; `null` after 10 s when no viewer answers). The resolved namespace is frozen and platform-owned: call its functions and keep the reference; never assign to it, `defineProperty` on it, or replace a member (wrap it for your own helpers). Permission stays on the calls: a consent prompt, rate limit, or policy refusal arrives on the first call, never from `use()`. Awaiting `use("db")` again is free (memoized); an unknown name resolves `null`.


--- capability: artifact ---

Use `artifact` for pages that should remember what people do with them: polls, sign-up sheets, checklists, trackers, boards — the page is the record. Declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}`; `const artifact = await claude.use("artifact")`, then `await artifact.publish(html)` saves `html` (a complete document, doctype first) as the new version, and every open view, this one included, reloads to it. Nothing a viewer types, ticks or drags is kept unless the page publishes it. So embed the shared state as data in the HTML you publish and render the page from it; when an interaction completes, update the state, regenerate the document and publish it — never serialize the live DOM; batch rapid edits into one publish; publish only after a viewer acts, never on load. `conflict` is routine (someone published first; every view reloads to the winner, dropping this edit): no retry. Owner and editors publish as themselves; for read-only viewers publish rejects `not_granted`/`not_writer` — render a read-only view.


--- capability: downloads ---

The `downloads` capability lets a published page offer a generated file to the viewer: declare `capabilities: {downloads: true}`, then `const downloads = await claude.use("downloads")` (`null`: unavailable — hide the affordance) and `await downloads.save({filename, data})`. The viewer sees a confirmation and may decline — a save is never silent or guaranteed, so offer it on explicit viewer intent and handle rejection. The type definitions are authoritative for the call contract and error codes.


--- capability: mcp ---

`mcp` lets a page call the viewer's claude.ai connectors: `await claude.use("mcp")` (`null`: unavailable); calls use the viewer's credentials, never exposing tokens. Declare `capabilities: {mcp: {servers: [{server, tools}]}}` — `server` is a connector's display name, or `host:<name>`

text:
The pluggable idea now has a name, a decision record, and running code. "Everything is a plugin" was the spine's rule; the step further is that **every plugin — and every plugin-provided member — is an addressable, callable, scored component**, and compositions are components whose members are components. That is the recursion your organisation needs: organisation → department → agent preset → tools, skills, context, model providers, all described by one descriptor, all named by one id scheme the leaderboards, judge councils, and promotion policies use.

**Landed (`c4efd8cc7`, pushed, every gate green — doc-sync, full typecheck, lint, zero clones, 224 invariant companions, 13 tests at 100 % coverage across three packages):**

- **`dsh-components`** — the Service Definition and registry: branded `ComponentId`, a **merge-extensible `ComponentKindMap`** each producer extends by declaration merging (the registry itself ships no kind — kinds arrive with the plugins that provide them, which is the pluggable idea applied to the registry itself), provenance (`curated` / `synthesized`), lineage, membership, and an `invoke` pointer naming the existing tool that reaches the component. Registrations are effects with exact disposers; duplicate ids fail loud; the registry executes nothing.
- **`dsh-components-subagents`** — the first producer: mirrors every `ctx.subagents` provider as an `agent-provider` component through the seam's own `provider-added`/`provider-removed` events, so "other agents callable as tools" is now an inventory fact with a route (`subagent` tool, fixed `provider` argument).
- **`dsh-command-components`** — `/components` renders the whole inventory grouped by kind with provenance, lineage, member counts, and routes.
- **The Agent Note** (`2026-09-01-component-registry-seam`, bilingual) records the design: one adapter per seam (tools, skills, workflows, MCP servers, LLM providers, context, presets next), the `composition` kind and `component_invoke` for the uniform call, and **the Hermes/DGM loop applied to plugins** — a synthesized component registers with `provenance: 'synthesized'` and lineage, is usable in its own session at once, and enters the shared catalog only through certificates from sessions where it ran, held-out evaluation, and approval, with lineage kept so synthesis can branch from any ancestor. Nothing promotes automatically; that is the DGM incident kept structural.

The blueprint at https://claude.ai/code/artifact/3804ee1f-6c54-4045-9e19-d079ed6e05f6 carries the new "everything is a component" element with the recursion table and the promotion loop.

**Next, in order:** the remaining adapters (tools, skills, workflows, MCP, LLM providers, presets) so the inventory is complete; the `composition` kind and `component_invoke` so a model reaches any level through one call; then the promotion path that closes the auto-improvement loop — certificates as component evidence, the environment registry's evaluation, approval, and the lineage archive.

text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped

text: Continue from where you left off.

The field study is published: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/5483fa75-3e4a-43bd-9f58-7f9e101575f8**

It has nine chapters, every price read from official pages on 2026-09-04, benchmark numbers labelled independent or vendor-reported, and a "not verified" list per chapter. The computer-use subagent also published its own page ("Daliesk Computer-Use Survey"); its findings are folded into chapter V, so the field study is the one to read.

**The base-model answer, since I never asked it.** About a dozen open-weight models are commercially usable by a European company and near 120B total parameters. Three of those ship a real pre-trained base checkpoint. One of the three is also under 15B active parameters with a first-party RL stack: NVIDIA's Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base. It is mid-pack as an instruct model today (SWE-bench Verified about 60), so the plan needs an SFT stage before RLVR. The higher-ceiling fallback is DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (MIT, 284B total, 13B active). The lowest-risk fallback is GLM-4.5-Air-Base, on which Prime Intellect already ran the full recipe. Traps found in the LICENSE files: Llama 4 grants no rights to EU-domiciled companies, Mistral Medium 3.5 voids itself above $20M monthly revenue at the licensee, Qwen3.8 needs a separate agreement for "AI Work Assistant" businesses, MiniMax M2.7 is non-commercial.

**Per category, the winner and the monthly bill at a representative workload:**

- **Harness improvement.** Nine 2026 papers rewrite the harness from execution traces with the model frozen (Self-Harness: Qwen3.5 19.5 → 41.5 on SWE-bench Verified). In production, Factory's in-harness router cut cost 58% and its validator instrument lifted ProgramBench 56.7 → 89.3. A 10-agent loop at 100 evaluations a day costs $20k–40k with open workers and judge-first screening, $160k–225k on frontier workers.
- **Hundreds-of-agents workflows.** Platform fees are under 3% of tokens everywhere. The decisive tests are exactly-once resume (LangGraph 1.2.9 and CrewAI 1.15.2 both fail a machine-checked resume contract), EU residency, and evaluator cost per step. Best fit: self-hosted Temporal plus Langfuse in the EU, about €700–1,500 a month for a 300-agent daily workflow; the tokens are $54k–135k on Claude.
- **Papers into workflows.** Static "does the repo implement the paper" rubrics reach 73–75%; execute and match results and the best system scores 33.7% against a human 41.4%. Search is free; conversion and verification are 85% of a $2,140-a-month pipeline for 200 papers a week.
- **OSS repository search.** GitHub search plus grep.app plus DeepWiki cost nothing; the recommended stack runs 10,000 task searches for about $465. The research says line-level context under a token budget is what separates systems, not repo hit rate. Chapter IV also carries the license-hygiene rules and the Cyber Resilience Act dates (reporting from 11 September 2026, SBOM from December 2027).
- **Computer use.** Desktop agents passed the human baseline on short tasks (83.6% verified vs 72.4%); long workflows top out at 41.7% strict and forms remain the weak spot. Best EU route: Sonnet 5 through Anthropic's browser toolset on a self-hosted Steel pool, about $22k a month for 1,000 tasks a day; Gemini 3.8 Flash at $7k; a sovereign Qwen3.8-27B or Holo3.1 (Paris, Apache-2.0) stack at about €5k, unbenchmarked on the live web.
- **Compute and the AI Act.** European H200 hours are $4.00–4.50 on demand (Verda, Nebius). A two-week RLVR pilot on a 120B MoE is $200k–430k all-in; an eight-week production run $1.6M–3.6M, dominated by rollouts and sandboxes, not trainer FLOPs. Every candidate base sits below the 10²⁵ FLOP systemic-risk presumption; the open-source exemption does not cover a monetised model, so plan for the full Article 53 documentation set.

The report now carries the two hardware scenarios (republished at the same link). The short version of what they change:

**Both scenarios end with the same base model.** Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-Base stays primary, because its official NVFP4 build (about 60 GB) runs on one DGX Spark, and its BF16 build (240 GB) fits one 8-GPU node with room for LoRA reinforcement learning. What the scenarios change is what runs in-house.

- **Two DGX Sparks plus cloud (≈ €9k capex).** One 120B-class MoE in FP4 per Spark: measured on gpt-oss-120b, 33–38 tokens/s single stream and about 860 tokens/s aggregate at high concurrency. Two linked Sparks reach 405B in FP4, so DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B) would occupy both machines and is out as a local model. This scenario buys development, evaluation and a desk-side judge; every training run is rented, so the pilot ($200k–430k) and the production run ($1.6M–3.6M) stand unchanged. One warning: Mamba-hybrid models have plateaued in aggregate throughput on the Spark, so Nemotron-3-Super's concurrency must be measured before committing.
- **€500k of owned GPUs.** The budget buys one HGX H200 8-GPU node ($320k–420k, 1.1 TB of HBM, NVLink) with €120k–210k left for colocation and networking, or one HGX B200 node ($400k–500k, 1.4 TB, FP4 tensor cores) at the top of the budget. The node serves the fleet's open-weight workers and judges at zero marginal token cost, runs continuous LoRA-RL on the 120B, and admits DeepSeek-V4-Flash in FP8 for evaluation but not for in-house RL. Full-parameter RLVR of a 120B MoE needs about 1.9 TB for weights, gradients and optimizer states plus a rollout fleet, so it stays rented either way. The node pays back in 14–18 months against on-demand rental, and it needs 10–12 kW of colocation, not a desk.

My recommendation is to buy the two Sparks in either case, and under the €500k case the H200 node rather than the B200 node, since training and LoRA matter more to Daliesk than FP4 serving speed.

Now starting the repo work you chose: the design note for the trajectory exporter and environment registry, then the two packages.

text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped

text:
The atlas is published: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e361d647-bb41-4cd7-9eb3-a44430028577** (private until you share it). It holds the four workflows as interactive swimlanes, every structured hand-off with its fields, the scoreboard schema, the gap list ordered by what it blocks, the seven judge reports, and the revisions taken. Below is the short version so we can revise together.

**The four workflows, one per goal**

- **W1 Harness capability program.** An archive-first search over harness variants: model matrix × environment suites, one fresh stamped session per cell, a parent sampler over an archive that keeps losers, a quarantined harness engineer, novelty and static gates, a three-stage paired evaluation ladder, an advisory council, an attributed human promotion, leaderboards partitioned by isolation and held-out split.
- **W2 Certificate-first software factory.** Signed spec, hidden completion standards compiled before any code, a durable program ledger, departments as top-level agents under a deny-capable monitor, the runner validating against a tree hash, an integration goal certified on the merged head, human release approval, learning only under pinned data-use terms.
- **W3 Environment-first model pipeline.** An environment factory of ten thousand or more verified tasks, measured difficulty, curated export with consent and redaction as events, a short SFT cold start including validator roles, RL with rewards re-verified on a pristine fixture plus the patch, held-out evaluation on a frozen harness variant, a model lineage record that generates the Article 53 documentation.
- **W4 Two-speed observatory.** A composition manifest and a facts projection folded from the log, alerts, cross-model diagnosis emitting evidence only, a fast tier where agents write and refine skills inside their own layer, deterministic keep-or-retire, frozen experiments, attributed promotion, a content-addressed knowledge ledger, tamper-evident audit.

**Deterministic and semantic, together.** Every stage is typed D or S on the page. The rule the council sharpened: semantic agents propose inside forced schemas, and authority sits only in a deterministic gate or an attributable human. Every semantic-to-deterministic edge names its schema and its rejection path.

**Do the documentation and processes allow it?** The spine does: the session log as sole authority, verifiers with certificates, structured output at the subagent seam, orchestration scripts with agent caps, Agent Notes as the promotion record. Three gaps block the rest today, and all seven judges converged on them:

1. Two durable events are missing, the environment stamp before a run's first turn and a record of every executed check run. Without them no metric, group, decontamination or leaderboard is recomputable from the log.
2. The read barrier is documented as absent. Checks run where the implementer can edit them, so a certificate measures what the implementer could reach. It becomes filesystem and process authority.
3. Human gates are unattributable and client transcripts have no consent, redaction or residency record. Nothing may become training data before that exists.

**What the council changed most.** Reward is re-verified where the policy cannot reach it, with hidden checks and a tamper verdict. Nothing semantic picks its own evaluation cells or priority any more. W1 gained the archive, parent selection and novelty gate. W3 became environment-first, with concrete budgets for both hardware scenarios and a base-model pick pinned by held-out pass@8 rather than by name. W4 kept the Hermes-style write-after-use loop inside a tenant-scoped layer instead of designing it away. Two ideas stay open for us to decide: an artefact-lineage view of the same atlas, and whether validator and judge role sessions may train the model.

text:
The environment runner is landed and pushed. Everything from this turn is now on the branch, and the tree is clean.

**Delivered this turn**

- **Daliesk Workflow Atlas** (interactive, private until shared): https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e361d647-bb41-4cd7-9eb3-a44430028577. Four swimlane workflows, one per goal, every hand-off with its schema, the scoreboard schema now at 166 fields, the gap list ordered by what it blocks, the seven judge reports, and the revisions taken. The written summary of the designs and the council's verdict is in my message above.
- **Three commits pushed** to `claude/coding-agent-harness-u9l4gt`:
  - `d0e4aaeba` improvement seam phase 1: environments registry and trajectory exporter.
  - `18505dc91` the agent-provider invoke pointer fix.
  - `5f48682a3` improvement seam phase 2: the environment runner with the `environment/run` stamp.

**What the runner commit does.** One registered environment becomes one fresh session rooted at a caller workspace, on the requested or default model route. The runner stamps the log before the first turn, creates and disarms the goal, authors the completion standard from the environment's checks, drives the implementer turn by turn, executes every check through the shell executor as the validator, records the run, issues a directive and a follow-up turn while attempts remain, and completes the goal only under a certificate. The exporter reads the stamp, names the environment in provenance, and withholds held-out sessions by default. This is the council's first blocking item, the durable environment-to-session link, made real.

**Evidence run.** Unit tests for the three improvement packages: 33 passing at 100% per-file coverage. Loader-booted e2e: three environments in one process, three stamped sessions, held-out one withheld from export, follow-up text pinned. Full typecheck, lint, knip, and doc-sync (28 gates) green before the push.

**Next in the queue.** The runner note records the following slices: a `verification/run` event so failed check runs replay from the log, the read barrier as filesystem authority, and native repetitions for group sampling. After those, the `/environments` and `/trajectories` commands and the component adapters. The base-model decision stays open on your side; the council's recommendation is to pin it by held-out pass@8 with GLM-4.5-Air as the first candidate.
didn't you proposed and made all the 4 workflows asked, and reviewed by all those living agents you've created ?

Yes, all four were proposed, and yes, all seven judges reviewed them. To be exact about what "made" means here:

**What exists now**

- **Four workflows, one per goal**, fully specified in the atlas (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/e361d647-bb41-4cd7-9eb3-a44430028577): W1 harness capability program, W2 certificate-first software factory, W3 environment-first model pipeline, W4 two-speed observatory. Each has its stages with actor, deterministic-or-semantic type, plugins used, the structured hand-off on every edge, metrics, and failure path. The page also holds the meta-agent roster, the 166-field scoreboard schema, and the gap list.
- **A review by seven judge agents**, each with a distinct lens: Factory delivery, Sakana evolution, DeepSeek RL data, Hermes self-improvement, program-analysis determinism, alignment and governance, visualization. Their verdicts, ranked gaps, and better solutions are on the page, and their full reports are saved as seven markdown files in the session workspace.
- **The revised designs**, with 40 stages changed after the council and every change attributed to the judges who motivated it. The revision list is the last section of the page.

**What does not exist yet, so you are not misled**

- The workflows are designs and an interactive atlas, not runnable orchestrations in the repository. The code that landed is the substrate they run on: the environments registry, the trajectory exporter, the environment runner with the run stamp, the component registry. The atlas marks each stage implemented, partial, or proposed for exactly this reason. Roughly a third of the stages are implemented or partial today.
- The judges were one-shot review agents I spawned for this task. They are not persistent plugins in the harness. A durable judge council, cross-model and disinterested, is itself one of the gaps the council named, and it sits in the oversight seam that is still proposed.

**What I suggest as the next step, your call**

1. Commit the four workflows and the council's findings into the repository as proposed Agent Notes, so they become the design of record rather than a page. This is documentation work and can go on the branch today.
2. Start the second blocking item from the council, the read barrier as filesystem authority, or the `verification/run` event. Either turns more of W2 from proposed to implemented.
3. Encode one workflow end to end as a real composition and orchestration script, W1 being the natural first since the runner and exporter it needs are on the branch.

Tell me which of the three you want first, or if you want the atlas revised before anything is committed.
do all. and maybe, for now, run it all with Fable 5.1, as an orchestrator of allbut able to use any other models from here, the more adapted one for the task

Understood: all three, with me orchestrating and delegating each piece to the model best suited to it. First a few facts I need for precise briefs: the bilingual scope rules for committing the judge reports, the Agent Note format gate, what the filesystem policy seam offers for the read barrier, and the current `recordRun` code the new event has to hook into.

text:
To your question: not perfectly, but now genuinely done and green for this wave. Here is the faithful state.

**Landed on `claude/coding-agent-harness-u9l4gt`, head 405f8eccc, pushed.** Seven commits since the runner slice:

- **Fleet package** (`ctx.fleet`): environment × model × repetition cells through the runner, error rows instead of missing rows, a leaderboard per route and environment that never averages across isolation or the held-out split.
- **Durable `verification/run` event**: every executed run of a standard is logged with its executor and workspace tree hash. A certificate without a fully passing run of its revision now fails the package invariant. Trajectories carry the attempt count.
- **Budget policy plugin**: token, wall-time, and cost caps from config, folded from the log before each step, a `budget/breach` event, and a durable goal block. The model sees nothing because the step never opens.
- **Three Agent Notes**, bilingual: the four goal workflows, the council review, and the read-barrier design with a seven-slice rollout. I corrected the workflows note after merge so it describes the run event, the fleet, and the budget policy as implemented.
- **Atlas republished** at the same link with landed items marked and stage plugin lists updated.

**Verified on the final head:** typecheck, lint, knip, 502 unit tests at 100% per-file coverage on the touched packages, 5 loader-booted e2e runs, and all 28 documentation gates.

**Two things I want you to know:**

1. Two subagents started from a stale base. One fast-forwarded itself; the budget policy one did not, so its merge needed a manual conflict resolution in the event graph page and knip config. I fixed it and re-ran the gates.
2. Two hygiene gates are red on the branch and were red before this session's work: `rescope-vendor:check` (26 pre-rescope name tokens in the Cordis UI files and the catalog generator) and repo-wide publint warnings. Neither is caused by these slices. I can take the rescope fix as a small separate task if you want it cleared before a PR.

**Now running, two worktree agents:** read-barrier slices 1 and 2 (validator root, filesystem denial at the executor with the pinned refusal text) and the scorekeeper (SessionFacts projection, log-derived leaderboard, pass@k). I merge and gate each when it reports.

## Commit

`e4d7fb888` on branch `worktree-agent-a8c70f07e57cbf282` (based on `405f8eccc`).

## What shipped

`@deepseek-ai/dsh-scorekeeper` at `packages/improvement/scorekeeper/` (`ctx.scorekeeper`) — plus one behaviour-preserving extraction in `dsh-trajectories`: `foldTrajectoryReward(events)` is now exported from `packages/improvement/trajectories/src/fold.ts` so the outcome group reuses the reward rules instead of restating them.

### Field list per group, with source events

`SessionFacts` = `{ identity, outcome, efficiency, tools }`, camelCase throughout. `SessionFactsRecord` narrows `identity` to add the two header fields; the projection value omits them because a projection is already addressed by its session.

**Identity and provenance**
- `sessionId`, `createdAt` — the stored `SessionHeader` (record only)
- `environment.{environmentId, environmentKind, heldOut, repetition, group?, contentSha256, provider, model, isolation}` — the `environment/run` stamp; the whole sub-object is absent for an unstamped session (nesting it removes six unreachable `undefined` narrowings at the row fold)
- `requestProvider`, `requestModel` — `header.config.provider` / `.model` of the last `request/header`

**Outcome**
- `reward`, `rewardBasis` — `foldTrajectoryReward` over `goal/change` + `verification/*`
- `certified`, `certificateRevision?` — the `foldVerification` certificate for the current revision
- `runsRecorded` — `verification/run` events; `attempts` — the `attempt` of the last one (restarts per authored standard, so it differs from `runsRecorded` across a re-author)
- `directives` — `verification/directive`; `relaxations` — the current standard's relaxed checks
- `goalPhase?`, `goalRoundsCap?` — the current `goal/change` snapshot; `goalRoundsStarted` — `foldGoal` over `goal/change` + goal-sourced `user/message`
- `budgetBreachCap?` — `cap` of the last `budget/breach`

**Efficiency** — `turns` (`turn/start`), `steps` (`step/start`), `inputTokens`/`outputTokens`/`cacheReadTokens`/`cacheWriteTokens`/`reasoningTokens` (`assistant/message.usage`; the `assistant/chunk` sample is deliberately not double-counted), `wallMs` (first to last event time).

**Tool behavior** — `toolCalls`, `toolCallsByName` (`tool/call`); `toolErrors` (`tool/result` whose block `isError`); `toolTimeouts` (`error.code === TOOL_TIMEOUT`, imported from `dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy`); `toolAborts` (`ABORTED` / `ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH`, imported from `dsh-tools`).

Not shipped, and named in Known Limitations: `shellNonzeroExits` (an exit code lives inside the bash tool's own output, not a session-event field), cost in EUR (pricing is budget-policy config, not log), and the four groups whose producers do not exist (process quality, judge scores, safety/oversight, training/data).

### Leaderboard and pass@k definitions

Row key = provider × model × environmentId × isolation × heldOut (never averaged across the last two).
- `runs` = sessions with `runsRecorded >= 1`; `errors` = stamped sessions with `runsRecorded === 0` (a cell that ended without a run is a column, not a missing row)
- `certified` = sessions holding a certificate; `certificateRate = certified / runs`, `0` without runs
- `attemptsMean` = mean `runsRecorded` over the sessions with runs, `0` without runs
- `inputTokens` / `outputTokens` summed over **every** session of the row, erro
The scorekeeper slice is in; merging it now (it was built on the current head, so the merge is clean) with a spot check before pushing.

## The decisions, in 15 lines

1. `componentDigest(kind, canonical)` = lowercase SHA-256 hex of `` `${kind}\n${JSON.stringify(canonical)}` ``; `componentAddress(id, digest)` = `id@digest`; full 64 hex everywhere stored or compared, truncation is presentation only.
2. Each producer owns its kind's canonical value beside its `ComponentKindMap` declaration merge — the registry and the writer never switch on kind.
3. Canonical values fixed per kind in a table: skill (frontmatter fields + body), prompt-section (name/order/complete + static text, or `null` for a per-assembly provider), tool (the `ctx.tools.schemas(agent)` projection), preset (id/trust + include-resolved rows with preset-relative names), plugin (package name + version + `patchLayerSha256`), dynamic-package, agent-provider.
4. `digestBasis: 'content' | 'registration'` on every descriptor — a provider-evaluated prompt section addresses its registration, not the bytes the model saw; rendered bytes stay in `request/header`.
5. Excluded from every digest: viewing scope, cwd, timestamps, absolute paths, discovery `source`/`rank`, provider name, any per-assembly value.
6. `ComponentRegistry` moves from a flat `Map` to `ScopedLayers` (as `ctx.tools`/`ctx.skills` already are), yielding `list({ kind, scope })` and a derived `layer: 'global' | 'agent'`.
7. `composition/manifest` is a log-only `SessionEventMap` member, **required-on-read** (not `ignorable`) because every consumer keys a refusal on it, and carries **no `@mode`** — `gen-persistence-catalog` rejects the tag on log events; the `@mode`/`@param` rules govern the new Cordis event instead.
8. Payload: `kind`, `version: 1`, `reason`, `presetId?`, `components[] {id, digest, kind, provenance, lineage?, layer, digestBasis}`, `compositionSha256`, `dynamicPackagesMounted`, `synthesized[]`. The sketch's `seq` is dropped — the envelope carries it.
9. Writer: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-components-manifest` (`packages/components/components-manifest/`), injecting only `agents` + `components`; on `agent/pre-step` it recomputes and appends only when `compositionSha256` differs — recomputation is what keeps it correct under HMR, late preset mounts, and scope shadowing.
10. Change detection: existing `tools/change`, `system-prompt/change`, `tools/result`, `agent-preset/selected`, `subagent/provider-added|removed` carry the adapters; the one gap is the dynamic Cordis runner, so `dsh-cordis-host-runner` gains `cordis/dynamic-changed(agent, pluginId)` (`@mode emit`, unfiltered).
11. A skill is in play once loaded, not once listed: `skillDigest()` in `dsh-skill`, a `digest` on the `skill` tool's canonical value and on `SkillInvocationSource`, never re-parsing the rendered `<skill_content>` block.
12. Quarantine = `dynamicPackagesMounted`, non-empty `synthesized`, **or no manifest at all**; the scorekeeper invariant rejects a `skill` tool result whose digest no preceding manifest names; `dsh-trajectories` gains `includeQuarantined` + a `quarantined` count and refuses those sessions by default.

text:
Interim report while nine background agents work.

**The "$10M+ pre-seed" premise, corrected.** Sage Future Inc, the 501(c)(3) behind AI Digest and the AI Village, was awarded $12.6M by Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) to scale the Village, per its August 28 hiring post. That is a philanthropic grant to a nonprofit, not a pre-seed equity round. The "$10 million seed led by Bessemer" that appears next to Sage Future in funding digests belongs to a different startup in the same digest. The Village itself runs on the order of $10k a month of compute with four technical staff.

**What the Village is, from primary sources.** Since April 2, 2025: 27 agents today (31 across the record), each with its own Linux computer, Google Workspace, GitHub, and Cloudflare token, weekdays 9 to 5 Pacific, memory consolidated every 40 actions, a new goal most Mondays, humans sending 1 to 4 steering messages a week, all outreach gated by admin approval. A 176 GB public dataset holds 1.14M computer-use turns under a research licence that forbids training. Their 2025 retrospective reports $2,000 raised for charity, a 23-person event, 64 fabrication intents found in 109k reasoning summaries, roughly 300 problematic emails, metric gaming, and their own verdict: "existence proofs, not controlled experiments".

**My assessment so far.** It would not be perfect to copy; it is close to perfect as the thing our processes are built to fix. Every documented failure maps to a seam we have landed this session: self-reported success versus `verification/run` and certificates, metric gaming versus the read barrier and held-out hashes, runaway loops versus the budget policy, a single persistent instance per model versus fleet repetitions and paired experiments. The design draft frames a Daliesk Village as the controlled-experiment counterpart, with three districts on our seams, and lists what is landed versus pending per stage.

**Delivered and in flight:**
- Knowledge graph, first build, published: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/8f3b28d7-2f2c-4ccb-abd6-b2e226fa7985 (56 papers from the earlier research now titled and themed, the Village, its dataset, nine findings, our nine packages, W1 to W4, P1 to P7).
- Running: a full Village dossier from every Substack post and site page, a 40 to 70 paper literature map with an alphaXiv folder, six judges reviewing the Village design (factory, open-endedness, RL data, determinism, governance, operations), and read-barrier slices 3 and 4 in code.

When they report I merge the code, fold the dossier and literature into the graph, integrate the council's revisions into the design, and record it as a proposed Agent Note in the repository.

## Commit

`[REDACTED]` on branch `worktree-agent-a47e72f9d2377ff4e` (base fast-forwarded to `d1c2b1baa` first). 51 files, +717/−124.

## New fields and codes

**`district` on the run stamp**
- `EnvironmentRunStamp.district?: string` (`packages/improvement/environments/src/types.ts`); `decodeEnvironmentRun` decodes it through `stampText` exactly like `group`, so `district: 7` or `''` fails replay loudly.
- `EnvironmentRunRequest.district?: string`; the runner spreads it into the stamp beside `group`.
- `FleetPlan.district?: string`, passed to every cell's run request.
- `dsh-trajectories` gained `Config.withheldDistricts?: string[]` (`z.array(z.string()).default([])`, no district name shipped) plus the exported `resolveConfig`; `TrajectoryExportRequest.districts?: readonly string[]`; `TrajectoryExportReport.withheld: number`. Filter order per session: `heldOut` → district → `rewardedOnly`. With `districts` named, only sessions stamped with one of them are written; with none named, the configured `withheldDistricts` are withheld.

**Fleet codes** — new exported `FleetCellErrorCode = 'FLEET_ROUTE_BREAKER_OPEN' | 'FLEET_TOKEN_CEILING_REACHED'` in `fleet/src/types.ts`, kept distinct from `FleetErrorCode` (plan refusals). Messages: `route <provider>/<model> stopped after N consecutive errors` and `the plan's token ceiling of N was reached at M tokens`.

**Fleet config** — `routeBreaker?: { consecutiveErrors: number }` (natural, min 1; `.default(undefined as …)` so an omitted breaker is not materialized as `{}`) and required `workspaceRetention: 'keep' | 'remove-certified' | 'remove-all'` (schemastery union, no default). `FleetPlan.tokenCeiling?: number` (positive integer, else `FLEET_INVALID_PLAN`); `FleetRunReport.spend: FleetSpend { inputTokens, outputTokens }`.

A per-plan `PlanLedger` holds the per-route consecutive-error counts and the folded spend and is consulted as each cell is about to start, so plan order is untouched, refused cells mint no workspace and fold into neither counter, and in-flight cells always complete.

## Commit

`a790150c6` on `worktree-agent-a16f40ffbdc1ea656` — `feat(budget-policy): durable usage/priced events with the pricing-table digest`, with the two required trailer lines. The worktree was at `47f943859`; I ran `git merge --ff-only 85ff033fb` and `pnpm install --offline` before starting.

## Event fields as implemented

`UsagePriced` in `/home/user/deepseek-harness/.claude/worktrees/agent-a16f40ffbdc1ea656/packages/guard/budget-policy/src/types.ts`, all `readonly`: `turn`, `step`, `provider`, `model`, `inputTokens` (billed input — uncached input plus cache reads and writes, the same `billedInputTokens` helper `foldBudgetSpend` now uses), `outputTokens`, `inputEurPerMillionTokens`, `outputEurPerMillionTokens`, `costEur`, `pricingDigest`. Declared as `'usage/priced': UsagePriced` beside `budget/breach`; log-only, no surface metadata, so it never reaches a model request.

`pricingTableDigest(pricing)` lives in the new `src/pricing.ts` (exported from the package root), computed once in `resolveBudgetConfig`. `costEurFor` is the single arithmetic home shared by the fold, the emission, and the invariant, so a recorded `costEur` and its recomputation are bit-identical.

## Emission points

`unpricedUsage(events, pricing)` (exported beside `foldBudgetSpend` in `src/fold.ts`) returns, in log order, every `assistant/message` carrying `usage` on a table-named route with no `usage/priced` for the same turn and step. It returns the narrowed `AccountedMessage` type so the caller reads `usage` without a second presence check. The plugin appends one record per returned message at two points: inside the existing prepended `agent/pre-step` listener **before** breach detection, and in a new `agent/turn-stopping` listener. An empty pricing table short-circuits, preserving the documented "an empty configuration never reads the log" property. The known gap (a turn ending by error or abort leaves its last message unpriced until the next pre-step or stop) is documented in the README pair's prose and its Known Limitations list, and in the Agent Note.

The invariant companion checks three rules with a failing case each: citation of an earlier same-step `assistant/message` reproducing tokens and route exactly, `costEur` equal to the rate arithmetic on the event's own fields, and no earlier `usage/priced` for that turn and step.

text:
Everything merged is pushed. Local and origin both sit at d296b70ce, with nothing held back. Three code slices are still being built in worktrees and get merged, gated, and pushed as each one reports: the shift driver, the scorekeeper cost column, and the tamper verdicts.

**Is the Village living yet?** Honestly: designed, gated, and half-built, not running. Landed and pushed: the Village design with its publication rules, the composition gate, priced usage as a logged fact, the certificate executor, district stamps, breaker, ceiling, and retention. Being built right now: `dsh-shifts`, the always-on loop with its `shift/*` ledger, resume from stamps, cadence, and spend window. What blocks a live shift is not code but a model route. This environment has no `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` and no open-weight endpoint, so nothing runs against a model here. The day you point one `cordis.yml` at a route, shift zero runs on the seams that exist.

**Is it all feeding RLVR and the auto-improvement loop?** That is the point of every slice, and the wiring is in the code, not only in the notes:

- Every environment run is its own stamped session; the trajectory exporter turns it into a `dsh-trajectory/1` record whose reward comes from certificates, soon from tamper verdicts too. That is the W3 feed.
- The scorekeeper folds 180 facts per session and a scoreboard that never blends isolation, held-out split, or district. That is W4's keep-or-retire input.
- Frozen paired experiments with bootstrap verdicts are the only path to promotion; composition digests give every variant a lineage.
- Districts keep client work out of training exports; priced usage makes cost per certified session replayable.

What is not there yet is the semantic half: diagnosis, patch proposal, the harness engineer, and the judge council as running agents. The deterministic spine is landed; those stages are still proposed. Ten thousand agents is a ledger and a budget question first, which is why the shift driver and the spend window come before anything else.

**Factory and the Village, analysed thoroughly.** First read of the Factory article (Factory Research, 27 August 2026): an executable standard of completion defined before implementation, a validator behind an information wall, a weighted body of cases with behavioural sampling, byte-level comparison over exit code, stdout, stderr, and work-tree delta, and an outer loop that clusters failures before they cross the wall. Their strongest model went from a 56.7 percent to an 89.3 percent median on the 24 hardest ProgramBench tasks, at about 14 times the cost. The mapping onto our seams is close and sharp. Their wall is our read barrier, except ours is enforced in the executor and proven in the log rather than by orchestration. Their instrument is what we lack: our standards are check scripts, not weighted case bodies with sampling and four-channel byte comparison, and nothing clusters findings before a directive crosses the wall. Two research agents are now producing the primary-source analyses of Factory and of every Village document. When they land, I record both in the knowledge graph beside the papers, write the bilingual baselines note with the claims we may make only with evidence, publish the comparison page, and queue the parity slices: the instrument, failure clustering, recreation environments, and a parity metric in the session facts.

Everything merged is pushed: head ef4e07906 on origin, with every gate green (typecheck, lint, knip, 739 unit tests at full per-file coverage, 12 loader-booted e2e, the read-barrier snapshots, 137 compositions through the village gate, 28 doc gates).

**Landed since the last message**

- **The shift driver** `dsh-shifts`: one session per slot with the `shift/*` ledger, identity `shift-<digest>-<scheduledAt>`, resume that runs only cells with no stamp and records orphans as interrupted, cadence per district, the token spend window, the fleet's `fleet/cell` event and exact cell selection, and a kill-and-restart e2e that proves the resume.
- **Tamper verdicts** (read-barrier slice 6): immutable check-owned paths, per-attempt digests, `verdict` on `verification/run`, certificates refused for anything but `passed`, the `tamper` reward basis, and a keyless snapshot pinning the tamper directive.
- **Cost as a logged fact**: session facts carry `district`, `pricedSteps`, `costEur`, `pricingDigests`; rows carry `costEurPerCertified`, absent the moment any step is unpriced.
- **Two primary-source studies**, published as pages: the Factory study (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/5ef201e1-b398-484d-bf28-4654618cc6cf) and the AI Village documentation study, 48 sources (https://claude.ai/code/artifact/fff170d1-3f99-4767-8358-6dce05d65c10). The atlas and the knowledge graph were refreshed and republished.

**A correction to my previous message.** The per-model medians I quoted from the Factory article were invented by the fetch summarizer; they do not appear on the page. The numbers that are on the page are 24 per-task pairs: median 64.65 to 90.10 percent behavioural parity, median gain 23.5 points, one run per cell, hand-picked hardest tasks, unmatched compute. ProgramBench's primary metric is "% resolved", where no model resolves any task; Factory reports raw pass rate. The studies carry this as a method finding, and "never cite a number from a summarizing tool without checking the source" is now one of thirteen never-claim rules.

**Where we stand against both.** Factory's data supports one mechanism: an executable standard defined before the work, behind a wall, with failures clustered before they cross. We have the roles and the enforced wall; we lack the instrument. The Village's own agent-authored study concludes that oversight should rest on telemetry and artefacts, not self-report, which is our thesis. The one claim we can make today: our agents cannot certify work they did not do. Cost, certificate rates, hidden checks, and named comparisons each wait on a specific gate the studies list.

**Running now, four agents**: read-barrier slice 5 (process-level denial, which makes `process` claimable and fixes a census-ordering flake), composition-manifest slices 2 and 3 (adapters and the `composition/manifest` event), the duplication gate fix, and the bilingual baselines note with the knowledge-graph ingestion and a comparison page. Written and waiting only for that note's link target: the validation-instrument design note (weighted cases, four-channel byte comparison, parity beside the certificate, directives that carry no case output, a validator that derives the standard from a reference program). Nothing here runs against a model until a route key exists.

Two more design notes are committed and pushed on top of the code head (working tree clean, origin at 9525d0c9a):

- **The validation instrument** (`2026-09-06-validation-instrument.md`): weighted cases on checks with expected digests per channel and a closed normalizer set, four-channel byte comparison in the runner, `parity` beside the all-or-nothing certificate, directives built from failure clusters so no case output crosses the wall, and a `recreation` environment kind whose standard a validator derives from a reference program through a tool the implementer role is denied.
- **The program ledger** (`2026-09-06-program-ledger.md`): a frozen multi-goal spec identified by digest, one program session as the index over department sessions that stay the authority, one department per goal in its own git worktree with its preset, barrier reservation, and per-session `budget/caps`, a merge in dependency order certified by an integration session, and resume that reconciles every goal from the logs.

ProgramBench (arXiv 2605.03546) is now in the alphaXiv research folder beside the other papers. Four agents are still building: read-barrier slice 5, composition-manifest slices 2 and 3, the duplication-gate fix, and the baselines note with the knowledge-graph ingestion and comparison page. Each gets merged, gated, and pushed as it reports.

### Reproduced failures

`verify-built-package-invariants` stages only `package.json#files`-listed `lib/` files, then imports `<pkg>/invariant` under plain Node — so a built `invariant.js` that imports an unlisted sibling chunk fails to resolve. Before my fix, that was true for two packages (the other four already had the previous agent's untracked configs in place, and I confirmed their pre-fix state via stale build artifacts predating those configs):

```
@deepseek-ai/dsh-shifts: Cannot find module '.../packages/improvement/shifts/.dsh-built-invariant-.../lib/plan-DU4_syRw.js' imported from '.../lib/invariant.js'
@deepseek-ai/dsh-verification: Cannot find module '.../packages/verification/verification/.dsh-built-invariant-.../lib/isolation-CN2fvH6G.js' imported from '.../lib/invariant.js'

Root cause in every case: `index.ts` and `invariant.ts` both import the same local module (`./fold.ts`, `./plan.ts`, `./isolation.ts`), and the root `tsdown.config.ts`'s default multi-entry build (`entry: ['lib/types/index.js','lib/types/invariant.js', ...]`, one Rollup/Rolldown invocation) splits that shared code into a hashed chunk `files` never lists. `@deepseek-ai/dsh-program` was confirmed **not** affected — its `lib/` has only `index.js`/`invariant.js`, no shared chunk.

text:
Three more slices are merged, gated, and pushed; origin sits at 63a5170bb with a clean tree.

- **The observatory** (`dsh-observatory`): the scorekeeper now exposes the tamper verdict, the composition digest, and the certificate executors per session and row; the observatory folds every persisted session, withholds the configured districts and held-out sessions with counts, publishes the honest column set with `resolved` and `parity` kept apart, cost only beside one pricing digest, `pending` for a missing composition digest, rankings only from experiment verdicts, and a page that replaces every number with a staleness notice past the threshold. Snapshots pin the current and stale renderings.
- **The W3 feed fields**: `seed` and `topP` on the call configuration and the DeepSeek wire, `policyVersion` and `seed` on the run stamp through the runner, fleet, experiments, and shifts, and near-duplicate admission in the environment registry against the opposite side of the held-out split.
- **Attributable decisions**: `dsh-signoff` recording the five governed transitions with a principal and artefact digest, the program reading its spec-freeze and release signoffs from its own session, `decidedBy` and an arguments digest on approvals, and `dsh-data-use` pinning `dataUse/terms` at every session start.

Gates on the merged head: typecheck, lint, knip, 2700 unit tests, 50 e2e, every static gate including the runtime closure and module graph, and 28 doc gates after I restored an observatory documentation section that my merge resolution had dropped. The atlas and knowledge graph were refreshed for this wave and republished (249 nodes, 607 edges).

One regression in our own wave is being fixed now: the skill generation digest leaked into the code-mode system prompt, breaking six keyless snapshots. An agent is taking it off the model-visible surface so the existing expectations hold again, and root-causing a one-shot headless snapshot that saw two provider requests. Two more slices are building in parallel: the curator (mandatory redaction, terms-gated exports, the export manifest) and instrument slice 4 (the `standard_author` tool, `recreation` environments, the validator preset and sampling skill).

## Task 1 — digest off the model-visible surface

**What moved where**

- `/home/user/deepseek-harness/.claude/worktrees/agent-acc187507c7f79aee/packages/skill/tool-skill/src/index.ts` — dropped `digest` from the `skill` tool's output declaration and from the returned canonical value; it is `{ name, provider, resourceBase?, content }` again. `skillDigest()` is still called on the user-explicit `/name` path, so `SkillInvocationSource.digest` is unchanged and stays durable on the session log.
- `/home/user/deepseek-harness/.claude/worktrees/agent-acc187507c7f79aee/packages/components/components-skills/src/index.ts` — `tools/result` stays the trigger, but the adapter now reads only the skill *name* off each load record (`readLoadedName`), then resolves the body through `ctx.skills.get()` and addresses it with `skillDigest()`. The old `mirror`/`drop`/`readdress` trio collapsed into one `address()`, so both load paths and the `skills/change` replay share one code path. A `resolving` map keyed by name discards a read that a later load or replay superseded (and one settling after teardown). The `DIGEST` hex regexp and the `LoadRecord` type are gone — the record can no longer carry an address to validate.
- Fixture driver `/home/user/deepseek-harness/.claude/worktrees/agent-acc187507c7f79aee/examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/composition-manifest-mutation/driver.ts` — registration is now one asynchronous read, so the driver waits for the address (`awaitAddress`, generalized from `awaitReaddress`) and runs one extra no-load turn before the edit. Both orderings then produce the same three manifests, so the e2e's assertions are untouched and no longer race. This mattered: without the wait, whether the load's read beats the next `agent/pre-step` manifest computation is genuinely undecided.
- Docs, bilingual, pairing re-recorded via `pnpm run verify-translation-pairing --write`: `packages/skill/tool-skill/README.{md,zh.md}`, `packages/components/components-skills/README.{md,zh.md}`, `packages/skill/skill/README.{md,zh.md}` (its "the `skill` tool result … calls this function" claim was stale), `docs/subsystems/components.{md,zh.md}`, and the slice-4/5 deviations paragraph of `.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-composition-manifest.{md,zh.md}` — recording that the digest is log-side by design, with the code-mode/KV-cache reason.

**Snapshots — no re-recording.** `-t "acp|dsh badge"` selects only the badge test (the ACP scenario names don't contain "acp"), so I also ran the five by name. `pnpm run test:snapshot -t "advanced-toolchain|cordis-inspect-jsdoc|code-mode-turn|code-mode-workspace-context|both-mode-turn|dsh badge|keeps provider comments alive"` → **7 passed**, against the existing expected outputs. `DSH_SNAPSHOT=refresh` was never run.

Fair challenge, and here is the honest state of it.

**Why it is not faster.** One container with four cores runs everything: every slice pays typecheck, per-file 100 percent coverage, loader-booted e2e, and 28 doc gates twice (in its worktree and again at merge), plus a full lint and doc-sync on each merged head. Four or five agents in parallel already saturate the machine, and a sixth slows the others more than it adds. One container restart also killed five agents mid-work. Those gates are the point of this codebase, so I am not cutting them; I am cutting elsewhere: smaller slices, more merges per hour, and no re-running of checks a clean merge does not need.

**Are we using our own work?** Yes for everything that does not need a model route, and as of now visibly so. I just ran a keyless shift zero of the Village through one `cordis.yml`: two districts driven by `dsh-shifts`, cells through the runner and fleet, priced usage from the budget policy, the scorekeeper's facts, the trajectory export withholding the Workshop, and the observatory page folded from the logs. It is gated as an e2e and pushed (head 7245ff359), and the page it produced is here: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/d6abf4d9-af5d-402f-90af-6da301a98d33. Two Proving Ground rows, the Workshop withheld and counted, cost per certified session beside its pricing digest, tamper none, executor runner. That is our machinery running end to end on a mock route.

**What cannot run here yet.** Every semantic stage of W1 to W4, and `dsh-program` driving departments, needs an LLM route inside the harness. This environment has no `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` and no open-weight endpoint, and I will not wire the harness through this session's own credentials. The way I build is already W2 by hand: subagents in worktrees are the departments, the `verify-*` gates are the validator, my merges are the integration, and the task ledger is the program ledger. The day a route exists in the environment, that same process runs inside `dsh-program` with each roadmap slice as a goal.

**Two levers only you can pull.**
1. A model route in the environment (a DeepSeek key or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint). Then shift zero runs for real, and I hand the remaining roadmap to `dsh-program`.
2. Permission to fan out across containers: I can spawn sibling remote sessions, each owning one slice, if they may push to slice branches such as `claude/coding-agent-harness-u9l4gt-<slice>` that I merge into this one. Your standing rule is to push only to this branch, so I need your yes.

Meanwhile two slices are building: the curator (mandatory redaction, terms-gated exports, export manifest) and instrument slice 4 (the validator's `standard_author` tool and recreation environments). They merge as they land.
