# Artifact runtime capabilities

A published Artifact page can declare **runtime capabilities** — abilities the claude.ai viewer grants the page at open time — by passing `capabilities: {name: config}` to the Artifact tool. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. Declaration gestures: **omitting** `capabilities` on a redeploy carries the stored declaration forward unchanged (and preserves the artifact's stored contract pin); an **empty object** `{}` is the explicit clear-all; a **non-empty object** is a full-set declaration (anything stored but not restated is revoked). Moving a republished artifact's runtime version is a deliberate gesture — pass `contract: 'latest'` to upgrade, or a specific version to pin or roll back — never a side effect of editing.

**Available capabilities:** `artifact`, `db`, `downloads`, `mcp`, `room`, `sample`, `self` — the complete set of capability names you may declare. Anything not listed is unavailable to this user.

Runtime contract 0.2.41


Capability namespaces live behind `claude.use(name)`: `const db = await claude.use("db")` resolves the capability's namespace, or `null` when this view cannot run it (not served, not granted, or failed to load — indistinguishable by design). Branch on `null` and design for absence. `window.claude` carries only `use`: no `window.claude.db`, `.room`, or `.artifact` member is ever promised, so never read one — render the page without them and light features up when the promise resolves (later, never within your script's first run, and unordered with DOMContentLoaded; `null` after 10 s when no viewer answers). The resolved namespace is frozen and platform-owned: call its functions and keep the reference; never assign to it, `defineProperty` on it, or replace a member (wrap it for your own helpers). Permission stays on the calls: a consent prompt, rate limit, or policy refusal arrives on the first call, never from `use()`. Awaiting `use("db")` again is free (memoized); an unknown name resolves `null`.


--- capability: artifact ---

Use `artifact` for pages that should remember what people do with them: polls, sign-up sheets, checklists, trackers, boards — the page is the record; data kept server-side, or seeded or read back by Claude, is `db`. Declare `capabilities: {artifact: {}}`; `const artifact = await claude.use("artifact")`, then `await artifact.publish(html)` saves `html` (a complete document, doctype first) as the new version, and every open view, this one included, reloads to it. Nothing a viewer types, ticks or drags is kept unless the page publishes it. So embed the shared state as data in the HTML you publish and render the page from it; when an interaction completes, update the state, regenerate the document and publish it — never serialize the live DOM; batch rapid edits into one publish; publish only after a viewer acts, never on load. `conflict` is routine (every view reloads to the winner, dropping this edit): no retry. For read-only viewers publish rejects `not_granted`/`not_writer` — render a read-only view.


--- capability: db ---

`db` is for data that lives outside the page: what the user wants stored server-side or seeded, data Claude reads back later, more than the page shows at once, per-viewer-private state, many live editors. If the page itself can be the record, republish (`artifact`). Seed or inspect the store from here with `write_db`/`read_db`; never hardcode seed rows in the page. A realtime JSON document store: `const db = await claude.use("db")` (`null`: unavailable). Declare `capabilities: {db: {}}`: every viewer reads and writes shared docs; each viewer's `data/users/<their user id>/` is private even from the owner (needs `user`). Two direct answers.

**Model agnosticism.** The harness is model-agnostic by construction, and the fork ships it that way: the LLM seam is a Service Definition with providers for DeepSeek, for pi-ai (which covers Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and others behind one adapter), and the mock and replay routes; the subagent seam has out-of-process providers for Claude Code, Codex, any ACP server, and the harness SDK. Two things kept you from using me on your workflows here, and one of them is mine to fix:

- This container holds no API key for any provider, so the harness's own agent loop had no route. I checked a moment ago whether the Claude Code CLI itself runs authenticated as a child process here. It does: `claude -p` answered.
- The Proving Ground's cells were driven only through the LLM seam, never through the subagent seam, so an external coding agent could not yet be the implementer of a cell. That is the gap. The fix is one slice, the external implementer: the runner hands a cell's task to the Claude Code provider (or Codex, or any ACP agent) inside the cell's workspace and validates it exactly as today, with our checks, certificates, tamper digests, and the census recording which agent did the work. It launches as soon as the instrument slice that is editing the runner right now lands, and then I run the first real, non-mock cells in this container with Claude as the implementer. On your own machines nothing blocks you today: point `dsh-llm-pi-ai` at Anthropic or OpenAI with a key, or DeepSeek with its key.

**The transcripts.** Nothing produced is lost: every slice is in git with its notes, tests, and gates. The process record also exists and is now in your hands: I delivered my full session log (33 MB of JSONL) and all 173 subagent transcripts with their tool results as a two-part archive above (rejoin the parts; the digest starts 468f5a87ddea9e48), and an agent is producing a compact analysable dataset from them (one record per agent, one per message, statistics, provenance). Two honest facts about that data:

- They are Claude Code transcripts, not `dsh-trajectory/1` records. They carry no run stamps, hidden checks, or certificates, because this week's work ran through Claude Code rather than through our harness, which had no route.
- Under Anthropic's usage policy, Claude outputs may not be used to train a competing model. These transcripts are analysis material: failure taxonomies, process mining, environment synthesis with invented entities, the same use we allowed ourselves for the Village dataset. The RLVR corpus for the Daliesk model must come from the harness's own certified runs on routes whose terms allow it. That is precisely what the Proving Ground, the exporter, and since an hour ago the curator produce, and they start producing it the day a permitted route (a DeepSeek key or an open-weight endpoint) is in the environment.

So the week built the machine that records the data correctly, it did not lose data the machine could have recorded. The curator merge is pushed (head c118400d9, all gates green). Running now: instrument slice 4 and the transcript dataset; queued next: the external implementer.

Status while the three slices build: the transcripts are in the repo, the snapshot Routine is armed, and Claude-inside-the-harness is being built on three fronts in parallel.

**Pushed** `4c693ee2f` on `claude/coding-agent-harness-u9l4gt`. It adds `data/transcripts/2026-09-06-build/`: the verbatim Claude Code session tree of this whole build (orchestrator plus 71 subagent transcripts plus 28 overflow captures, 142.6 MiB, per-file SHA-256 in `raw/manifest.json`), the compact dataset regenerated from it, bilingual READMEs, and two tools. The collector refuses credential-shaped content unless each match is accepted by digest (only two fixture placeholders were accepted), splits files above 40 MiB, and is idempotent. All 28 doc gates and both tracked-file gates passed. One thing to know: the raw tree carries your account e-mail where the harness's context reminders quoted it, 77 times. No credentials.

**Nothing lost from here on.** A Routine named "Hourly transcript snapshot into data/transcripts" (`trig_01U95vY7sQkhEm4SxJyKQacw`) fires into this session every hour, re-collects, commits, and pushes only when something changed.

**Running now, three opus agents in worktrees:**
- External implementer: the Proving Ground runner delegates a cell to Claude Code through the subagent seam and still authors the standard, runs the checks, and issues the certificate. Includes a real-run fixture that also exports facts and trajectories and renders the observatory.
- The bridge: a new MCP tool server exposes the harness's own tools to the external agent with its built-in tools disabled, so every call passes the read barrier, fs policy, approvals, and the session log.
- Program departments delegated to external agents, same certificates.

On model-agnosticism, verified: the LLM seam already reaches Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and any gateway through `dsh-llm-pi-ai` with an API key. A subscription has no API key, so it enters only through Claude Code, which is exactly what these slices wire in. I also confirmed the CLI authenticates from a credential-scrubbed environment here, so the real runs will work.

Next, once they land: merge, gate, push, then run the first real Proving Ground and program with Claude Code as implementer and publish the observatory.

text:
Everything is pushed. Branch head is `ed540d141`, origin matches, and the working tree is clean. Here is the full picture.

## Ruflo: it looks like us, it is not us, and mostly yes

The GitHub agent read ruflo from a shallow clone of the 2026-09-05 commit, not from its README. The verdict is in `.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-07-ruflo-comparison.md` with a criteria matrix and file-level evidence.

- **What it is.** A meta-harness over Claude Code. Its own instructions say the vendor's Task tool does the work, so Claude Code owns the loop, the context, and the permissions. Ruflo adds a queen coordinator with consensus over coordinator state, a mutable memory store consolidated by a model, 35 plugins, and about 309 MCP tools.
- **Its headline numbers do not hold.** The SWE-bench 84.8 percent claim has no harness, seed, model, or date anywhere in the tree, and its own ADR-171 says it has no SWE-bench oracle. Its own audit found a speedup computed from a random number and a benchmark suite timed with sleeps. Its nightly loop shipped 4 of 80 issues, then ten accepted pull requests nobody merged.
- **Where it beats us today.** Distribution through the plugin marketplace, signed per-platform attestation with a publish-blocking check, and a binding standard for published numbers.
- **What we do that it cannot.** Reconstruct exactly what the model saw, gate completion on a certificate behind the read barrier, and decide a change with a frozen paired experiment. Coverage thresholds in its test config are commented out.
- **Adopted from it.** A signed witness over the composition manifest, reporting rules in the observatory's render path, and the fate of a shift's output on its ledger. The caution stands too: certificates do not create the human capacity to land output.

## The three-month sweep, now a plugin

Three research agents swept GitHub, Hugging Face, and arXiv for 2026-06-01 to 2026-09-07 under one brief. Their 104 items merged to 103 in `data/knowledge/2026-q3/`, split over eight authored theme skills with generated reference tables and every file's digest. The pack is mounted as the only skill root in `examples/headless-agent/tests/fixtures/knowledge-pack/cordis.yml`, and the keyless e2e proves the catalog lists every theme and one loads through the skill tool. A stale pack now fails `doc-sync`. The decisions it produced are in `2026-09-07-q3-knowledge-sweep-decisions.md`.

| Finding | Number | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clean Apache-2.0 base in the 120B class, European, with a fine-tune-and-republish precedent | 119B total, 6.5B active | Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603, Leanstral-1.5 |
| SWE-bench Verified tasks that accept a verified-incorrect patch | 28.5 percent | arXiv 2606.16062 |
| LLM-authored hardening tests that fail on the gold patch | 61.9 percent | arXiv 2606.16062 |
| Share of multi-turn input that is cache reads | 74 to 94 percent | Skill Blocks, arXiv 2608.14943 |
| Token cost spread between harnesses at equal pass rate | up to 41.9 times | The Scaffold Effect, arXiv 2607.22585 |

Two findings bound the plan. TRL's Harbor documentation states that an agent installed inside a sandbox emits no policy tokens and cannot be RL-trained, so our LLM route is the capture boundary and delegated Claude Code runs stay measurements. And a European outfit already sells signed agent certificates to the clients we address, so our runner certificates need a signable export.

## Knowledge as a plugin and the KV cache

Partly yes. The mechanism is exactly the cache economy you describe: the catalog reaches the model once as a durable message after the reusable prefix, each theme reduced to a name and a capped description; a body loads only when the model calls the skill tool; the item tables load on demand; a pack change appends a replacement catalog instead of rewriting history; and the skill digest stays off the model-visible surface so the prefix never moves on an edit. i am trying to understand what you are doing : and more importantly, is it really SOTA?

Fair question, and it deserves a plain answer in two parts.

## What is actually running

Three things produce the stream of messages you see.

- **A Routine you asked for.** Every hour it snapshots this session's transcripts into `data/transcripts`, commits only that directory, and pushes. That is the "nothing lost" guarantee, nothing more.
- **The live district.** Every 30 minutes the harness hands three small Node tasks to your Claude Code installation, restores the immutable tests, runs the checks itself, and issues or withholds a certificate. It has survived two container restarts and stands at 40 slots, 120 of 120 certified.
- **Today's main work.** A three-source sweep of June to September 2026, packaged as a knowledge pack the harness serves as skills, a code-level comparison with ruflo, and three notes with decisions. All pushed.

## Is it SOTA? Part by part, honestly

| Claim | Where we stand | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Log as sole authority, model-visible equals logged, replayable sessions | Ahead of ruflo, AI Village, and most open harnesses | Their state lives in mutable memory stores; ours is an append-only event log |
| Verification integrity: standard before work, runner-executed checks, restored fixtures, tamper digests, read barrier, blind judge | Design at or above the published bar; evidence thin | Prime Intellect calls sandbox-shared grading "mitigation, not a guarantee"; our live runs still use isolation none |
| Coding performance of the harness | Unmeasured | No SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench run exists for our harness with any model |
| Harness self-improvement loop | Substrate built, zero results | No paired experiment has ever promoted a change; the district's tasks are too easy to discriminate anything |
| The 120B model | Pre-data | Nothing trained; a base candidate and a recipe reading exist |
| Multi-agent roles on your subscription | One role proven at scale | The implementer role ran 120 certified cells; validator, judge, and departments ran only in keyless fixtures plus one real LLM-route run |

So the truthful sentence is this: **the architecture is state of the art on integrity and provenance, and the results are not state of the art on anything yet, because we have measured almost nothing that the field measures.** The district's 120 of 120 proves the pipeline works end to end and survives restarts. It does not prove capability, because slugify and a pagination fix cannot fail a competent agent. Ornith-1.5 shipped a model from the loop we are building, under MIT, with SWE-bench Verified 79 at 3B active parameters. LEGO-RL trains inside unmodified harnesses with token-exact capture; our LLM route logs messages, not token ids. Those are the two results a reviewer would hold up against us.

## What would make the claim defensible

1. **Run the harness on a public benchmark.** A Harbor adapter, then Terminal-Bench 2.x and SWE-bench Verified with two or three models, publishing certified rate and tokens per certified task. Without this, "best harness" is a design claim.
2. **Replace the toy tasks.** Import gold-validated environments such as the verified SWE-rebench cut or Terminal-Lego, at isolation process or host, and audit the reward with the 500 known-cheating traces before trusting it.
3. **Promote one change through an experiment.** One frozen paired plan with a held-out reliability estimate that promotes or rejects a real harness change. That is the first real result for goal 4.
4. **Capture tokens at the route and run one small RL pilot.** Even a LoRA pilot on a small model from our own certified runs turns goal 3 from a plan into evidence.
5. **Put the other roles on the subscription for real.** Validator, judge, and departments through the LLM route in the district, not only in fixtures.

Items 1 and 2 are the ones I would do next, in that order, because they decide whether the rest is worth building. Say the word and I start with the Harbor adapter and the environment import.

text:
**Status.** The bench smoke's failure is fully diagnosed and the fix is being built; the subscription is busy in the meantime.

**What was wrong with the harness-loop arm**
- The Claude Code LLM route described harness tools as prompt text and asked for tool calls inside a structured reply. Sonnet, opus and haiku all ignore that and emit a native `tool_use` for `bash` instead. The product answers "No such tool available", the model tries again, and the query dies at the two-turn bound. That is 11 of 12 queries in the smoke and 0 of 3 in isolated probes. An explicit instruction only helps on the second turn, wasting one API call per step, and haiku still breaks the JSON-string argument protocol.
- The fix is proven by a probe: the harness tools offered as real in-process MCP tools with capture-only handlers, one assistant message per query, no structured output. Sonnet twice, haiku and opus all made a native call on their first message, in 5 to 6 seconds per query.
- Two smaller defects also surfaced: the bench composition had no filesystem tools, and the model was never told the workspace is its working directory. Both are fixed and pushed.

**Landed and pushed** (commit `128e037bb`): all thirty bench tasks admitted, the composition fix, the bench end-to-end test, and the bilingual hypothesis-program note. Every doc-sync gate passed.

**Running now**
- Two opus agents in worktrees: the native-tool-use rewrite of the route, and a slice that forwards the cell's model to external implementers. Without the second one, product-loop cells silently ran the installation default. I measured that default as sonnet, so the current fleets are labelled honestly.
- Two product-loop fleets on the subscription over tier 2 and tier 3 tasks, two repetitions each, plus the district on its cadence. The first two tier-2 cells already certified.
- The roles-matrix agent is still on its later roles.

**Next**: merge the two slices, rerun the one-cell smoke until it certifies, then start E0 calibration and the harness-loop versus product-loop experiment on the same cells, and record every run under `data/proving-ground`.

## Branch and commit

- Branch: `worktree-agent-a47e32782b70b9955`
- Commit: `[REDACTED]` (94 files, +1178/−215). Not pushed.

**Worktree base correction:** the worktree was created at `47f943859`, which predates `packages/improvement` entirely — the slice's target files did not exist. I fast-forwarded the branch to `128e037bb` (the commit the shared checkout is on) before starting; that base carries no commits of my own.

## What was built

**Seam** (`packages/subagent/subagent`) — `SubagentCapabilities.model`, `SubagentStartRequest.model?`, and on `SubagentResult`: `reportedModel?`, `reportedUsage?`, `reportedCostUsd?`. I used the seam's existing flag-per-option table and its `UNSUPPORTED_CAPABILITY` code rather than a bespoke `SUBAGENT_MODEL_UNSUPPORTED`: the capability table's own JSDoc states a one-to-one flag↔option correspondence, and a second code for the fifth option would be unexplained asymmetry. `runsOutOfProcess` deliberately does not read `model` (same reason it ignores `harnessTools`).

**Providers** — `claude-code`: SDK `model` option → CLI `--model`, both modes; reads model from `system`/`init` and usage/cost from the terminal `result`, on completed/error/aborted paths alike; bridge mode also records `model` and `costUsd` on `bridge/end`. `spawn`/`fork`: select the model on the child's route, report it back. `dsh-sdk`: initializes its child runtime on it. `codex`/`acp`: refuse — verified in the pinned schemas that ACP's `NewSessionRequest` has no model field, and I could not obtain evidence for Codex's `thread/start` (no `codex` binary on this host, so its real-product tests self-skip and the README's compatibility rule forbids an unevidenced protocol field). **Open question for review:** the slice brief said "Codex has a model flag" — I documented the refusal plus what regaining it requires, rather than guessing a wire field I could not test.

**Runner** — resolves the model before `requireImplementer`, refuses a provider lacking the capability with a new `ENVIRONMENT_RUN_IMPLEMENTER_MODEL_UNSUPPORTED` before any agent exists, starts every child on the stamped model, and records `reportedModel`/`reportedUsage`/`reportedCostUsd` on `environment/delegation`. Per the version-mechanism note, an additive optional payload field is not a structural change, so `SESSION_FORMAT_VERSION` is unchanged.

**Scorekeeper** — `identity.implementerModel` and `efficiency.delegated` (tokens + `costUsd`), plus the matching zod wire schema so the projection does not strip them. Gained a `dsh-environment-runner` peer/dev dependency and tsconfig reference for the type-only event merge, following the existing `budget-policy`/`components-manifest` precedent; no tsconfig cycle results.

**Program** — one-line Known Limitation: its frozen `implementer` spec names no model, and giving it one changes every existing program id.

## Real-product evidence

`claude` on PATH; the keyless real-product suite ran and a new test proves the selection end to end: `--model dsh-start-selected-model` reaches the CLI's actual Messages request body (replacing the settings model), and comes back through `init`. Here is the account, then the goals, then what I propose to run.

## What happened, 2026-09-07 11:35 to 2026-09-08 11:35 UTC

**Volume.** 78 commits on the branch, 21 of them hourly transcript snapshots, 997 files changed, 137,857 lines added and 966 removed outside the transcripts. Eighteen run records and four folds now sit under `data/proving-ground/`. This session and its subagents consumed about 17 million output tokens and 8.4 billion cache-read tokens of the subscription, plus every bench cell.

**Built and merged, in order.** Knowledge packs as plugins (the Q3 sweep and the fortnight sweep with the Sakana routing deep-dive). The bench: thirty zero-dependency program tasks in tiers 2 to 4, then ten tier-5 tasks judged on hidden cases the implementer never sees, with an admission gate and a fairness audit that fixed three specification corners. The Claude Code LLM route rewritten to offer the harness tools natively, which removed the two-turn bound that had broken every role but the implementer. The roles matrix: implementer, validator, judge, program departments, and bridge each run once for real on the subscription. Delegated cells forward their model and record the child's reported spend. Frozen experiments whose arms name their implementer. Budget parity for delegated attempts. Session continuity on the route, verified by a real e2e where the second step reads more cache than it writes. The sealed cell: the read barrier denies a cell everything above its workspace, under bwrap, with a census tool. A craft-skills arm for the knowledge hypothesis. Three fixes found only by running: the delegated follow-up dropped the task prompt, the reserved check scripts dropped each case's argv, and the `process` claim is unprovable over the route because the route's own CLI spawn counts as an unenforced subprocess.

**Measured.** Every comparison is a certificate rate under the same runner on the same restored fixture.

| Question | Tier, cells | Result | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Harness loop vs product loop, same model | 2 to 4, 96 | 48 of 48 vs 48 of 48 | inconclusive, wall time level |
| Same, frozen experiment | 3, 36 | 18 vs 18 | inconclusive |
| Same, tier 5 audited, seed 2 | 5, 32 | 12 vs 11 | inconclusive, −0.0625 [−0.125, 0] |
| Small vs middle model | 3, 36 | 18 vs 18 | inconclusive, small model 2.3× steps and tokens |
| Middle vs large model | 3, 36 | 18 vs 18 | inconclusive, large model cheapest in tokens |
| One attempt vs three | 3, 18 + 18 | 18 vs 18 | null, no second attempt taken |
| One attempt vs three, tier 5 counterfactual | 5, 16 | 8 vs 11 | reject the cap, −0.1875 [−0.25, −0.125] |
| Knowledge pack mounted | 3, 18 + 18 | 18 vs 18 | null, pack never opened |

**What the measurements are worth.** Less than they looked at the time. A census run this morning found that in every harness-loop record one to fifteen cells changed directory to the run directory and read the plan, the log, and sibling cells; one tier-2 cell copied the other repetition's solution, one tier-5 cell wrote its whole solution into its sibling's workspace, and a third copy turned up in the harness-loop tier-5 record. Product-loop cells never left their workspace, but nothing enforced that either. The tier-5 attempts comparison was also two different instruments: the harness loop's second attempt kept its transcript, the product loop's second attempt was a fresh child holding only the directive. Both defects are now fixed and recorded, and every earlier record carries the census paragraph, but no number above is clean, and the tier-5 reruns under the seal are the first that will be.

**Operational losses.** The subscription's session limit hit at 04:10 and reset at 05:30; it killed two opus agents, two tier-5 experiments at 20 of 22 cells each, two product cells of the recorded tier-5 experiment, and the district driver. # DeepSeek Harness — Architectural Inventory & Gap Analysis

**Scope:** `/home/user/deepseek-harness` at HEAD. ~230 workspace packages across 50 groups, plus `apps/cli`, `apps/web`, `vendor/` (rescoped Cordis), `native/landlock-run`, `python/`.

---

## 1. Core loop and spine

### 1.1 What the loop is

`packages/core/agent-loop` is described as *"the only package in the harness that contains concrete loop logic"* — `packages/core/agent-loop/README.md:7`. The `Agent` interface, registry and `agent/*` event vocabulary live separately in `packages/core/agent` so that the driver is swappable (`packages/core/agent/README.md:5`).

Turn/step flow (canonical statement at `docs/architecture.md:67-82`), with the durable appends in the driver:

| Boundary | Source |
|---|---|
| `turn/start` append | `packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:255` |
| `step/start` append | `packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:279` |
| `step/end` append | `packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:292` |
| `turn/end` append | `packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:319` |
| `agent/pre-step` dispatch | `packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:235` |
| `agent/request` dispatch | `packages/core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts:439` |

Vocabulary is fixed in `docs/glossary.md:36-39`: **turn** = one drain of admitted input; **step** = one model request plus its tool executions; **round** = an outer *policy* iteration (goal round, Ralph round) that is explicitly *not* a synonym for a turn.

### 1.2 Documented extension points

Declared in `packages/core/agent/src/runtime-types.ts` (no dependency on the loop package):

- `agent/created` :159, `agent/disposed` :168, `agent/status` :178
- `agent/inbox/inserted` :186, `agent/inbox/claimed` :197, `agent/inbox/discarded` :205
- `agent/session-start` :217
- `agent/pre-step` :231 — waterfall returning `{kind:'reject'}` or `{kind:'enter', messages}`
- `agent/request` :244 — waterfall returning `LlmCallConfig`
- `agent/request-error` :260 — recovery waterfall returning `RequestErrorAction`
- `agent/turn-stopping` :278 — serial, no `next()`
- `agent/error` :290

Tool pipeline is a second family owned by `ctx.tools`: `tools/pre-execute` → registered monotonic `tools.guard()` → `tools/execute` → `tools/post-execute` → definition-owned `finalizeContent` → observe-only `tools/result` (`packages/core/tools/README.md:7`). Prompt assembly adds `system-prompt/assemble` (`packages/core/system-prompt/README.md`, "Live events"). Capability events (`fs/*`, `sandbox/*`, `llm/stream`, `session/event`, …) form the third family (`docs/architecture.md:59`).

The "where new behavior goes" table (`docs/architecture.md:108-127`) is the load-bearing routing map — 20 goals each mapped to a mechanism.

### 1.3 "Plugins, not loop changes" in practice

The rule is stated verbatim at `AGENTS.md:108`:

> **Plugins, not loop changes**: new behavior goes on documented extension points; changing `agent-loop` requires updating docs/architecture.md.

Reinforced at `packages/core/agent-loop/README.md:7` and enumerated at `packages/core/agent-loop/README.md:76-83` ("What belongs to plugins": hooks/policy, compaction, model-request recovery, sandbox/permission/plan mode, sub-agents, persistence, UI).

Evidence the rule actually holds:
- **Compaction** attaches at `agent/pre-step` (pressure) and `agent/request-error` (overflow repair) — `packages/compaction/compaction-basic/README.md:20-21`.
- **Plan mode** is logged per-agent state plus a prompt section — no loop branch (`packages/plan/plan-mode/README.md:7`).
- **Goals + Ralph** were built as two plugin policies specifically to avoid a loop core: *"There is no `packages/loop/` family, `LoopDriver`, `LoopId`, universal `StopCondition`, or model-facing generic `loop` tool"* — `.agents/notes/implemented/feature/2026-07-16-harness-level-loop.md:22`; rejected alternative at :108 ("Modify the concrete agent loop with goal or Ralph modes").

Source: https://factory.ai/news/what-it-takes-for-coding-agents-to-complete-large-software-tasks
(Raw HTML fetch was blocked by the site; content was extracted via multiple targeted WebFetch passes over the same cached page, with a final pass verifying every featured quote word-for-word. See "Extraction caveats" at the end.)

## 1. Publication info and core thesis

- **Authors:** Factory Research, Theo Luan
- **Date:** August 27, 2026 — "10 minute read"

**Core thesis:** Models are now excellent at problems with "compact, stable criteria for success" (math proofs, optimization), but large software tasks lack a pre-existing, executable definition of "done" — specs describe outcomes without saying what must be validated. A single agent judging its own work makes locally correct progress and stops early, not from lack of skill or budget, but because "it never established a complete account of what remained." The fix the article demonstrates: an independent, executable standard of completion, authored by the same model in a separate validator role before implementation begins, kept behind an information wall, and maintained until the work meets it.

## 2. Every distinct capability/technique/principle the article claims is required

### 2.1 An external, executable standard of completion (the central claim)
The article's conclusion: effective large software work requires "an external, executable standard of completion — one derived from the outcome, before implementation narrows attention, and kept current until the work meets it." "Establishing a whole outcome requires more than a list of requirements": a system needs (a) an inventory of what must be established, (b) procedures for establishing each part, and (c) current evidence that those procedures pass against the artifact being delivered. Requirements say what should be true; only executable procedures establish whether the work achieves it.

### 2.2 Define validation before implementation narrows attention
The standard must derive from requirements and relevant sources of truth *before* the task is decomposed into work items. Rationale: once implementation begins, checks the agent writes "inherit the scope of the work that produced them" — they can establish everything the agent thought to build but exclude "features, interactions, or constraints it never represented." Without a prior measurement, "an agent constructs one piecemeal as it works," and "every local judgment may be reasonable while parts of the whole remain unmeasured."

### 2.3 The standard may evolve but must never weaken to fit the artifact
Checks can be added, replaced, or refined as the system learns, but "the standard of completion must not quietly collapse around whatever has already been built." Operationally: the validator "can expand the instrument as it learns more about the reference, but cannot weaken or revise it to accommodate what the candidate happens to contain."

### 2.4 Role separation: orchestrator / implementer / validator
The system splits one agent into three roles, all the same model at the same reasoning level:
- **Orchestrator:** decides what to measure, adjudicates findings, "rejects noise or invalid measurements," turns remaining problems into directives, and decides when to ship.
- **Implementer:** investigates the reference and builds the candidate; never authors, runs, or sees the instrument.
- **Validator:** surveys the reference before implementation, builds and holds the instrument, measures successive candidates, and "groups failures by root cause."
The loop: orchestrator selects what to measure → validator tests the candidate and interprets failures → orchestrator adjudicates and directs → implementer advances the candidate.

## 1. Per-work findings

### 1.1 Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM)
- **Exact name:** arXiv: "Darwin Godel Machine: Open-Ended Evolution of Self-Improving Agents"; blog: "The Darwin Gödel Machine: AI that improves itself by rewriting its own code"
- **Date:** arXiv submitted 2025-05-29 (last revised 2026-03-12, v-latest); blog 2025-05-30
- **Links:** [arXiv 2505.22954](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954) · [blog](https://sakana.ai/dgm/) · [code](https://github.com/jennyzzt/dgm)
- **Collaborators:** Sakana AI + Jeff Clune's lab at UBC (authors: Jenny Zhang, Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Robert Lange, Jeff Clune). (Your "Vector" attribution is plausible via Clune's Vector affiliation but the blog only names UBC — flagged.)
- **Summary:** A coding agent (frozen foundation model + evolving harness code) that rewrites its own harness — tools, prompts, workflow code — and validates each self-modification empirically on coding benchmarks. Instead of hill-climbing on the single best agent, DGM keeps an **ever-expanding archive of interesting agents** and branches new self-modifications off *any* archive member (Darwinian open-ended search), which mattered: some low-scoring ancestors were instrumental stepping stones to the best final agents. **SWE-bench: 20.0% → 50.0%; Polyglot: 14.2% → 30.7%**, surpassing Aider's hand-designed agent. arXiv record updated March 2026 (no venue stated in the arXiv comment field).
- **Lesson (a) harness:** This is the master pattern — treat the harness itself as the mutable genome, gate every harness patch behind held-out benchmark evaluation, and keep an archive/lineage rather than a single trunk so you can branch from stepping stones and audit every change. Maps directly onto a plugin-based harness: self-modifications are plugin diffs with CI gating.
- **Lesson (b) RLVR flywheel:** 20→50% with **zero weight updates** quantifies how much reward lives in the scaffold; run harness evolution first so your RLVR rewards measure the model, not scaffold noise. DGM's archive of (harness-diff, benchmark-delta) pairs is itself verifiable-reward training data; the paper also reports improvements transferring across held-out models and languages (transfer claims from memory of the paper, not re-verified today — flagged).

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. text:
# Harness Improvement: systems, production harnesses, leaderboards, pricing (research memo for Daliesk, 4 September 2026)

All prices were read on **2026-09-04** from the URLs given; "vendor-reported" means the number comes from the model maker's own announcement or model card, not an independent run. Where an official page could not be rendered by my fetcher I say so and give the best substitute.

---

## Part A — Harness-improvement systems

### A1. Nous Research: Hermes Agent, Atropos, DataForge
- **What it is.** Hermes Agent (released 2026-02-25 per nousresearch.com/releases) is a self-hosted, long-lived personal agent with a messaging gateway (CLI, Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, etc.), FTS5 memory, Honcho user modelling, subagents, cron, and a "skills" system in which the agent writes reusable procedures from its own trajectories and refines them in use (skills follow the agentskills.io format; `/learn` distills a skill from a directory/URL/workflow). Atropos is Nous's RL-environment/rollout framework; DataForge is the graph-based synthetic-data generator (random walks over a DAG of struct-to-struct transforms with PDDL-style pre/post-conditions) described in the Hermes 4 technical report (Aug 2025) and used to make ~5M samples/~19B tokens for Hermes 4.
- **License/status.** Hermes Agent: MIT, 241.2k GitHub stars, 27,617 commits on main, v0.21.0 current (github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent). Atropos: MIT, but the repo was **archived 2026-07-04** ("no further updates, bug fixes, or security patches"), last release 0.3.0; no successor named. DataForge: no public repository (github.com/NousResearch/DataForge returns 404); it is an internal pipeline.
- **Evidence.** Adoption (241k stars in ~6 months) is the hard fact. The v0.18.0 "Judgment Release" (2026-07-01) added *completion contracts* for `/goal` (the standing-goal loop judges "done" against evidence, not model confidence), a per-profile *verification evidence ledger* of detected project checks, and a `pre_verify` hook; ~1,720 commits, 949 issues closed, 381 contributors in that release. Nous's "40% faster with 20+ self-created skills" claim is internal and unverified.
- **Pricing.** Nous Portal (portal.nousresearch.com): Free $0; Plus $20/mo ($22 monthly credits); Super $100/mo ($110 credits); Ultra $200/mo ($220 credits); top-ups $10–$200. The agent itself is free.
- **Reverse-engineer.** The *skill-distillation + evidence-ledger* pair: after a task succeeds, distill the trajectory into a named skill file, and gate "done" on a machine-detected verification record (test run, build, diff applied) rather than the model's claim. This is a cheap, weight-free self-improvement loop that also produces clean RLVR-style transcripts.

### A2. Sakana AI: DGM, ShinkaEvolve, AI Scientist v2, AI CUDA Engineer, Conductor/TRINITY, Fugu, RSI Lab/SIFT
- **Darwin Gödel Machine** (with UBC/Vector; arXiv 2505.22954). An archive of agent variants; each variant rewrites its own code and is kept if it scores better on SWE-bench/Polyglot. Reported 20.0%→50.0% SWE-bench and 14.2%→30.7% Polyglot. Apache-2.0, 2.3k stars (github.com/jennyzzt/dgm).
- **ShinkaEvolve** (ICLR 2026). LLM-driven program evolution with adaptive parent sampling, embedding-similarity novelty rejection (default threshold 0.99), and a *cost-aware UCB bandit over an LLM ensemble* for proposals; diff/full/cross patch types. Claims 150 samples to solve circle packing and a new MoE load-balancing loss. Apache-2.0; `pip install shinka-evolve`; Feb 2026 added Claude Code/Codex agent skills, May 2026 added headless-CLI mutation models (i.e., subscription coding agents as mutation operators).
- **AI Scientist v2.** Agentic tree search generating hypotheses, experiments and LaTeX papers; the *Nature* paper appeared 2026-03-26 (s41586-026-10265-5); one unedited workshop paper scored 6.33 at ICLR 2025 ICBINB (withdrawn before publication). ~6.5k stars.
- **AI CUDA Engineer** (Feb 2025). Claimed 10–100× kernel speedups; wit

Today is 2026-09-04. You are researching for Daliesk, a European open-source AI lab building a verification-first, plugin-based agentic-coding harness and planning a 10,000-agent AI enterprise where every agent, workflow, tool and knowledge source is a plugin and every task is scored.

CATEGORY: MANAGING AND IMPROVING MULTI-AGENT WORKFLOWS AT SCALE — workflows containing hundreds of agents working together, with step-level improvement of the workflow.

Cover at least: LangGraph + LangSmith (LangChain); CrewAI (+ AMP); Microsoft Agent Framework / AutoGen / AG2; OpenAI Agents SDK + AgentKit / Agent Builder; Anthropic Claude Agent SDK, Claude Code workflows/subagents, and any Anthropic managed-agent offering; Google ADK + Vertex AI Agent Engine; AWS Bedrock AgentCore; Azure AI Foundry Agent Service; durable-execution engines Temporal, Inngest, Restate, DBOS; Ray / Anyscale; Dapr Agents; kagent; n8n / Dify / Flowise; Prefect, Airflow 3; observability and evaluation layers used for step-level improvement: LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, Weights & Biases Weave, Helicone, Maxim, Galileo, Patronus. For each, determine whether it supports: durable state and replay, fan-out of hundreds of concurrent agents, human approval gates, per-step evals/scoring, A/B comparison of step variants, cost tracking, and self-hosting in the EU. Also cite 2025–2026 research on multi-agent effectiveness and failure (e.g., the MAST failure taxonomy 'Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail', Anthropic's multi-agent research system post, Google/DeepMind or Microsoft papers on orchestration, any 2026 benchmark of orchestration frameworks).

Use WebSearch and WebFetch to find CURRENT (2026) information; prefer primary sources (official docs, pricing pages, papers, GitHub READMEs). Do not rely on memory for anything dated after 2025; verify it. For each system record: name, maker; what it is (2–3 sentences); open-source or proprietary and exact license; evidence of quality (benchmarks, dates, adoption facts); pricing (exact plan names and prices from the official pricing page with URL and the date you read it: free tier, per-seat, per-trace, per-agent-hour, per-execution; 'quote-based' if enterprise-only); and 'what Daliesk should reverse-engineer from it' (one concrete mechanism).

End with: (a) a ranked shortlist for running and improving a 300-agent workflow with per-step scoring, (b) a cost model for 'a 300-agent software-delivery workflow run once per day for a month, 50 steps per agent, traces retained 90 days' with stated assumptions (platform fees only; model tokens separately estimated at 2M input + 200k output tokens per agent run at a stated frontier price), (c) open questions and anything you could not verify, (d) a Sources list with URLs. Be exhaustive and factual; no marketing language. Write at least 1800 words.
I'll start by loading the web research tools, then work through the systems in batches.

# Paper-to-workflow systems: landscape, evidence, pricing, and what Daliesk should copy

Research date: 2026-09-04. All prices were read on that date from the URL given unless marked "secondary" (aggregator/press) or "not verifiable". Benchmarks are cited with the paper/version date. Where a vendor page was blocked or JS-only, I say so.

## 1. Systems, one by one

### FutureHouse → Edison Scientific (PaperQA2, Crow/Falcon/Owl/Phoenix, Robin, Kosmos)

- **PaperQA2** (github.com/Future-House/paper-qa): Apache-2.0; CalVer, latest tag v2025.12.17. Agentic RAG in three tools: paper search → "gather evidence" (Retrieval-Contextual Summarization: each chunk is re-summarized against the query and given an LLM relevance score) → answer with in-text citations. Citation-graph traversal exists only in FutureHouse's internal build. Evidence: LitQA2 (248 questions, part of LAB-Bench) precision 85.2% ± 1.1, accuracy 66.0% ± 1.2, above PhD/postdoc biologists (arXiv 2409.13740, Sept 2024). Price: free software; you pay model tokens.
- **Platform agents**: launched 1 May 2025, free web + API, marketed for "automated systems that continuously monitor new publications". Crow = concise cited answers, Falcon = deep reviews (plus OpenTargets etc.), Owl = "has anyone done X", Phoenix = ChemCrow deployment. FutureHouse published a LitQA precision/accuracy chart versus frontier search models but the numbers are in an image; I could not extract them. On 5 Nov 2025 management of the platform moved to the for-profit spin-out Edison Scientific; the agents are now named Kosmos, Literature (175M+ papers/trials/patents), Analysis, Precedent, Molecules; Python client `edison-client` (`JobNames.LITERATURE`, `run_tasks_until_done`).
- **Robin** (arXiv 2505.13400, 19 May 2025; Nature vol. 651, 2026, s41586-026-10652-y): Apache-2.0 (github.com/Future-House/robin; Finch repo also public). Orchestrates Crow/Falcon (literature) and Finch (data analysis) into hypothesis → assay → candidate → RNA-seq interpretation; proposed ripasudil for dry AMD and ABCA1 upregulation; Nature abstract: 551 papers analysed in 30 min vs an estimated 294 human hours.
- **Kosmos** (arXiv 2511.02824, 5 Nov 2025; proprietary, platform only): structured "world model" shared between a data-analysis agent and a literature agent; per run up to 12 h / 20 cycles, ~200 rollouts, ~42,000 lines of code, ~1,500 papers. Independent scientists rated 79.4% of 102 sampled statements accurate: 85.5% for data-analysis statements (n=55), 82.1% literature (n=28), 57.9% interpretation (n=19). Seven reported discoveries (3 reproductions of unpublished/unseen work, 4 novel). Collaborators estimated 6.14 months (n=7, σ=2.49) of their work per 20-cycle run; the authors' own tally gives 4.1 expert-months. Limits stated in the paper: datasets ≤ ~5 GB, stochastic across runs, no mid-run steering.
- **Pricing (Edison)**: `edisonscientific.com/pricing` returned 404 on 2026-09-04 and `platform.edisonscientific.com/pricing` is private; docs say "generous free tier for academics" plus paid plans, no numbers. The official Kosmos announcement (edisonscientific.com/news/announcing-kosmos, 5 Nov 2025) states $200/run = 200 credits at $1/credit, "heavily discounted", founding subscribers lock $1/credit; an Edison grant page prices 20,000 credits at ≈100 Kosmos runs, consistent with 200 credits/run. Enterprise is quote-based (Incyte collaboration, 19 May 2026, terms undisclosed). Edison raised a $70M seed at ~$250M valuation on 19 Dec 2025 (TechFundingNews, secondary).
- **Reverse-engineer**: Kosmos's statement-level provenance contract, i.e. every sentence in the output cites either a notebook cell or a paper, and accuracy is reported per statement type (analysis/literature/interpretation). For Daliesk this means the agent's method card and generated tests should each carry a provenance pointer, and "interpretation" claims should be gated separately becau

Today is 2026-09-04. You are researching for Daliesk, a European open-source AI lab building a verification-first agentic-coding harness. One of its workflows must, for any specific coding task, search the open-source GitHub ecosystem for the best existing repositories, code, and documentation and bring them into an agent's context.

CATEGORY: SEARCHING OPEN-SOURCE GITHUB REPOSITORIES AND CODE KNOWLEDGE FOR A SPECIFIC TASK.

Cover at least: GitHub code search, GitHub Copilot coding agent, and the official GitHub MCP server; Sourcegraph (Cody, Deep Search, Amp); Greptile; Cognition DeepWiki and the DeepWiki MCP; Context7 (Upstash); Exa (neural search with a github category, Exa Research, websets); Firecrawl (developer search, agent-skills search); Tavily; Perplexity Sonar API; grep.app; Repomix and gitingest; Nia; Onyx; Octocode MCP; Zread; GitHub Spec Kit; model-native search tools (OpenAI web search tool, Anthropic web search and web fetch tools, Gemini grounding with Google Search) with their per-call prices; Hugging Face Hub search for models/datasets/spaces. For each: what it does, open-source or proprietary and license, evidence of retrieval quality (any 2025–2026 benchmarks or studies: repo-level retrieval for SWE-bench, CodeSearchNet successors, CoIR, SWE-bench Multimodal retrieval studies, Sourcegraph or Greptile published evals), pricing from the official pricing page (URL and date read; per 1k searches, per seat, per token; free tier limits), and 'what Daliesk should reverse-engineer from it' (one concrete mechanism: e.g., symbol-graph retrieval, wiki generation per repo, query rewriting, dedup by license).

Use WebSearch and WebFetch to find CURRENT (2026) information; prefer primary sources. Do not rely on memory for anything dated after 2025; verify it.

End with: (a) a ranked shortlist for 'given a task description, return the 10 best repos with license, activity, and the exact files to read, in under 60 seconds', (b) a cost model for '10,000 such task searches per month' with stated assumptions, (c) license-hygiene considerations for reusing found code in a European commercial product (GPL/AGPL contamination, SBOM, EU Cyber Resilience Act timelines) with sources, (d) open questions and anything you could not verify, (e) a Sources list with URLs. Be exhaustive and factual; no marketing language. Write at least 1500 words.

# Searching the open-source GitHub ecosystem for a specific coding task — tool survey for Daliesk

Date of reading for all prices and docs: **2026-09-04**. "Primary" = vendor page or paper read directly this session; "secondary" = third-party page, flagged where used. Repo licence/star/last-push figures come from the GitHub API (read 2026-09-04 through the GitHub MCP server).

I also ran live probes of five endpoints (GitHub `search_code`, Firecrawl developer search, HF Hub search, DeepWiki MCP, grep.app MCP, Context7 MCP) to check auth requirements and result formats.

---

## 1. Tool-by-tool

### 1.1 GitHub-native

**GitHub code search (REST `GET /search/code`, UI, MCP)**
- What: lexical search over default branches of public repos (and repos you can read), with `repo:`/`org:`/`language:`/`path:`/`filename:` qualifiers and `text_matches` fragments. Engine is Blackbird: sparse-gram index over "45 million repositories", "15.5 billion documents", "115 TB of code" deduplicated to ~28 TB unique content by sharding on Git blob object ID; per-shard p99 ~100 ms (GitHub engineering post).
- Licence: proprietary service.
- Quality evidence: none published as retrieval benchmarks; it is exact-match ranking, not semantic. Live probe: `"token bucket" rate limiter redis language:go` returned 1,716 files in <1 s (traefik, go-ramjet, ...).
- Pricing/limits (primary, docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search): free; "requires you to authenticate and limits you to 10 requests per minute"; max 1,000 results per query; only files <384 KB; default branch only.
- Reverse-engineer: **content-addressable dedup by blob SHA** — collapse identical files across forks before ranking, and use the blob hash as the cache key for anything you fetch or summarise.

**GitHub Copilot coding agent (cloud agent)**
- What: assign an issue / `@copilot` / MCP `create_pull_request_with_copilot`; the agent researches the repo, plans, edits on a branch, opens a PR. It uses Copilot's per-repository **semantic code-search index** ("initial indexing can take up to 60 seconds for a large repository", "no limit to how many repositories you can index", updates "within seconds"). It "can only make changes in the repository specified when you start a task" — it is not an ecosystem search tool.
- Licence: proprietary.
- Quality evidence: none published for its retrieval component.
- Pricing (primary, docs.github.com plans + usage-based-billing-for-individuals): Pro $10/mo (1,500 AI credits: 1,000 base + 500 flex), Pro+ $39 (7,000), Max $100 (20,000), Business $19/seat (1,900 credits/user/mo), Enterprise $39/seat (3,900). "1 AI credit = $0.01 USD"; the agent "consumes GitHub Actions minutes and AI credits", amount depends on model and tokens. Premium-request units are legacy for cohorts "who remained on legacy premium request-based billing after June 1, 2026" (docs); the switch date is otherwise reported by secondary press (Visual Studio Magazine, 2026-04-27).
- Reverse-engineer: **lazy per-repo semantic index built at first task with sub-minute SLO and incremental refresh** — index a candidate repo only when it enters the top-k, and reuse it across tasks.

**Official GitHub MCP server (`github/github-mcp-server`)**

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers - `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events

## Warning: API Drift - Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025-2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing - the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

| Area | Stale prior | Current API |
|---|---|---|
| Extended thinking | `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | On Claude 4.6+ models: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and **rejected with a 400** on Fable 5/5.1 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 / 4.8 / 4.7. Pre-4.6 models still use `budget_tokens`. |

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped

# Computer-use and browser agents, as of 4 September 2026

Published as a shareable page: **https://claude.ai/code/artifact/f551c219-0a4d-4e20-ad3f-625619ef228b** (private until shared). The full text follows.

**Method.** Every pricing page and leaderboard was read on 2026-09-04 from the URL cited in part (e). Evidence classes: VERIFIED (maintainer- or independently-run), SELF (vendor self-report), AGG (aggregator tracker — Steel leaderboard, BenchLM, LLM-Stats — sourced to a vendor post), OW (open weights). Pages that could not be fetched (OpenAI help centre, Perplexity, GitHub API, Manus pricing, the dynamic OSWorld table) are flagged and a secondary source is named.

## 1. Leaderboards, dated

**OSWorld-Verified** (369 desktop tasks; human 72.36%). Official table is client-rendered and unreadable; rows from Steel (10 Jul 2026), BenchLM (3 Sep), LLM-Stats (4 Sep), vendor posts. Pointer.ai states its **83.6% (Claude Opus 4.7)** and **81.5% (Sonnet 4.6)** are the two highest scores on the *maintainer-verified* track (2026, undated); everything above that is vendor-run. Qwen3.8-Max (hosted) 86.1 (3 Aug 2026, SELF; text-only checkpoint released under a custom licence); Claude Fable 5/Mythos 5 85.0 (9 Jun); Mythos Preview 85.4 (Steel) vs 79.6 (LLM-Stats) — conflict; Qwen3.8-27B 84.3 (5 Aug, **OW Apache-2.0**); Opus 4.8 83.4 (Steel) vs 82.3 (Anthropic footnote); GPT-5.6 Sol 83.2; Gemini 3.6 Flash 83.0; **Holo3-35B-A3B 82.6 (H Company, Paris, OW Apache-2.0)**; Sonnet 5 81.2 (30 Jun); Muse Spark 1.1 80.8; GPT-5.5 78.7; Opus 4.7 78.0; OSAgent (TheAGI) 76.26 (23 Oct 2025); Qwen3.6-27B 75.6 (OW); GPT-5.4 75.0 (5 Mar 2026); Kimi K2.6 73.1 (OW); Agent S3 72.6 with Behaviour-Best-of-N / 66.0 solo (OW framework); Muse Glimmer-30B 65.9 (OW, Aug 2026); OpenCUA-72B 45.0 (OW MIT, 100 steps); UI-TARS-1.5-7B 42.5 (OW).

4. **major** — No model or seed per run. `agentDefaultModel` "owns one process-wide default" (`core/agent-default-model/README.md`); `EnvironmentRunRequest` has only `environment`, `workspace`, `signal`. W1.1 × W1.3 × W1.8 needs one process per cell or a runner change.
5. **major** — Best-only promotion labelled archive. P5 says "keep the tree"; W1.9 and W4.7 keep one merged head. No store for evaluated-but-unpromoted variants, no parent sampler (DGM: ∝ sigmoid(score) × 1/(1+children); low scorers were stepping stones), no novelty rejection (ShinkaEvolve).
6. **major** — Snapshot gate versus text mutations. W1.7 returns snapshot failures "as the directive", but keyless snapshots pin model-visible text and re-recording needs a key plus review (`docs/testing.md`). Hermes writes a skill after use and refines it in use; the layered `ctx.skills` already provides that scoped layer ("usable in its authoring session's layer immediately", oversight note). 5. **major — distillation targets and scope are unrealistic** (W4.4, W2.10). A "context provider" is a code plugin; the data-driven channels are `agent-instructions` (AGENTS.md, digest-tracked) and `session-reference` (untrusted snapshots). "A `user` preset — authored by a person or by an agent — carries the same trust as shell access" (`agent-presets/README.md`): agent-written client knowledge becomes shell-trust fleet knowledge with no tenant boundary.

## What shipped

**`@deepseek-ai/dsh-budget-policy`** at `packages/guard/budget-policy/` (guard group, per `packages/README.md` — it sits beside the loop-hygiene and tool-timeout policies).

- **Commit:** `[REDACTED]`
- **Branch:** `worktree-agent-a69087076b766234a` (worktree base was `47f943859`, not the `70967151a` named in the task)

**Extension point:** the `agent/pre-step` waterfall, registered with `{ prepend: true }`. It is the earliest documented point before the next model request; prepending puts the budget decision ahead of any listener that would build request context or reserve continuation work. On a breach the listener does not call `next()` and returns `{ kind: 'reject' }` — the same stop `dsh-goal-round-driver` already uses — so the loop closes the turn with reason `blocked` having opened no step. `agent-loop` is untouched.

**Event payload** (`budget/breach`, log-only, declaration-merged in `src/types.ts`, registered in both persistence catalogs):

```ts
{ cap: 'maxInputTokens' | 'maxOutputTokens' | 'maxTotalTokens' | 'maxWallMs' | 'maxCostEur',
  measured: number, limit: number }
```

The e2e observes exactly `{ cap: 'maxOutputTokens', measured: 3, limit: 1 }`.

**Goal seam:** `ctx.goals.block(agent, ref, { code: 'budget-exhausted', message: 'Session budget <cap> exceeded: <measured> of <limit>.' })` — a real blocking operation exists, it is durable and disarms continuation, so no goal-round driver resumes the goal. `goals` is read via `ctx.get('goals')`, not `inject`: a hard inject would silently disable the entire budget when unsatisfied.

**What the model sees on a breach:** nothing. The decision precedes the step opening, so no prompt section, tool schema, tool result, or message text is added and no model request is made. The README states this in the canonical Model Experience section, and the loader-booted e2e proves the absence (one `assistant/message`, one turn ending `blocked`, zero goal rounds).

**Folding:** derived from the log only — `assistant/message` `usage` (billed input = uncached + cacheRead + cacheWrite; `assistant/chunk` samples deliberately ignored to avoid double-counting), priced per message against its own `provider/model` provenance, and wall time as the span between the log's first and last event times. That makes every measurement a pure function of the events preceding the record, which the `./invariant` companion recomputes independently (cost excepted, since pricing is not in the log — it checks only `measured > limit` there).

text:
Done. Clean tree, no model identifiers, all gates green.

## Commit

`e4d7fb888` on branch `worktree-agent-a8c70f07e57cbf282` (based on `405f8eccc`).

## What shipped

`@deepseek-ai/dsh-scorekeeper` at `packages/improvement/scorekeeper/` (`ctx.scorekeeper`) — plus one behaviour-preserving extraction in `dsh-trajectories`: `foldTrajectoryReward(events)` is now exported from `packages/improvement/trajectories/src/fold.ts` so the outcome group reuses the reward rules instead of restating them.

### Field list per group, with source events

`SessionFacts` = `{ identity, outcome, efficiency, tools }`, camelCase throughout. `SessionFactsRecord` narrows `identity` to add the two header fields; the projection value omits them because a projection is already addressed by its session.

**Identity and provenance**
- `sessionId`, `createdAt` — the stored `SessionHeader` (record only)
- `environment.{environmentId, environmentKind, heldOut, repetition, group?, contentSha256, provider, model, isolation}` — the `environment/run` stamp; the whole sub-object is absent for an unstamped session (nesting it removes six unreachable `undefined` narrowings at the row fold)
- `requestProvider`, `requestModel` — `header.config.provider` / `.model` of the last `request/header`

**Outcome**
- `reward`, `rewardBasis` — `foldTrajectoryReward` over `goal/change` + `verification/*`
- `certified`, `certificateRevision?` — the `foldVerification` certificate for the current revision
- `runsRecorded` — `verification/run` events; `attempts` — the `attempt` of the last one (restarts per authored standard, so it differs from `runsRecorded` across a re-author)
- `directives` — `verification/directive`; `relaxations` — the current standard's relaxed checks
- `goalPhase?`, `goalRoundsCap?` — the current `goal/change` snapshot; `goalRoundsStarted` — `foldGoal` over `goal/change` + goal-sourced `user/message`
- `budgetBreachCap?` — `cap` of the last `budget/breach`

**Efficiency** — `turns` (`turn/start`), `steps` (`step/start`), `inputTokens`/`outputTokens`/`cacheReadTokens`/`cacheWriteTokens`/`reasoningTokens` (`assistant/message.usage`; the `assistant/chunk` sample is deliberately not double-counted), `wallMs` (first to last event time).

**Tool behavior** — `toolCalls`, `toolCallsByName` (`tool/call`); `toolErrors` (`tool/result` whose block `isError`); `toolTimeouts` (`error.code === TOOL_TIMEOUT`, imported from `dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy`); `toolAborts` (`ABORTED` / `ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH`, imported from `dsh-tools`).

Not shipped, and named in Known Limitations: `shellNonzeroExits` (an exit code lives inside the bash tool's own output, not a session-event field), cost in EUR (pricing is budget-policy config, not log), and the four groups whose producers do not exist (process quality, judge scores, safety/oversight, training/data).

### Leaderboard and pass@k definitions

Row key = provider × model × environmentId × isolation × heldOut (never averaged across the last two).
- `runs` = sessions with `runsRecorded >= 1`; `errors` = stamped sessions with `runsRecorded === 0` (a cell that ended without a run is a column, not a missing row)
- `certified` = sessions holding a certificate; `certificateRate = certified / runs`, `0` without runs
- `attemptsMean` = mean `runsRecorded` over the sessions with runs, `0` without runs
- `inputTokens` / `outputTokens` summed over **every** session of the row, errored ones included (deliberately wider than the fleet's reported-cells-only sum; documented)
- `stats` (`EnvironmentStats`) = `{groups, samples, passAtK[]}`. A batch is the sessions of the row sharing a stamp `group`; for a batch of `n` samples with `c` certified, pass@k is the unbiased `1 - C(n-c,k)/C(n,k)` evaluated as `1 - Π(n-c-i)/(n-i)`; the row value is the mean over batches with `n >= k`, and a `k` no batch reached is absent. `k` list is `Config.passAtK` (default `[1]`, sorted and de-duplicated).

## Plan digest and group scheme

`planDigest(plan, thresholds)` (`packages/improvement/experiments/src/plan.ts`) is SHA-256 hex over canonical JSON of: a format version, the two arm routes in role order, the environment ids **sorted**, the repetition count, and the four thresholds (`bootstrapResamples`, `confidenceLevel`, `minimumDelta`, `cellTokenCap`). `tokenBudget` is deliberately outside the digest — it bounds what a deployment pays for, not what the comparison measures. `workspaceRoot`, `signal`, and `sink` are not digested. A plan may carry a `digest` the caller froze earlier; a value unequal to the recomputed one is refused as `EXPERIMENT_PLAN_NOT_FROZEN` before any fleet call.

Groups are `experiment-<digest>-baseline` and `experiment-<digest>-candidate`, passed as each arm's `FleetPlan.group`, so the runner writes them into every session's `environment/run` stamp. `parseExperimentGroup` reads them back; the package invariant owns the `experiment-` namespace and rejects a stamp claiming it without a 64-hex digest and a known role.

## Statistic and verdict

A repetition pairs when both arms reported it (a fleet error outcome leaves its partner `unpaired`). Per environment: `baselineRate`, `candidateRate`, `delta = candidateRate − baselineRate`, `attemptsDelta` (mean), and summed `inputTokenDelta` / `outputTokenDelta`, all over paired repetitions alone. Each interval is a percentile bootstrap: a resample draws, within every environment, as many paired deltas as that environment holds, with replacement; the overall statistic is the mean over every drawn delta, so an environment weighs by its paired count and an empty one contributes nothing. Draws come from mulberry32 seeded with the 32-bit FNV-1a hash of `<digest>:<environmentId>`, so a result replays. Verdict: `promote` when the overall interval's lower bound exceeds `minimumDelta`, `reject` when its upper bound is below zero, `inconclusive` otherwise (including no pairs); `promote` is tested first so a negative `minimumDelta` is not order-dependent.

## Commit

`[REDACTED]` on branch `worktree-agent-aebe381f4ba63be3f` (based on `475de9978`). Three new files: `.agents/notes/proposed/architecture/2026-09-05-composition-manifest.{md,zh.md,i18n.yaml}` — 118 lines each side, no package code.

## The decisions, in 15 lines

1. `componentDigest(kind, canonical)` = lowercase SHA-256 hex of `` `${kind}\n${JSON.stringify(canonical)}` ``; `componentAddress(id, digest)` = `id@digest`; full 64 hex everywhere stored or compared, truncation is presentation only.
2. Each producer owns its kind's canonical value beside its `ComponentKindMap` declaration merge — the registry and the writer never switch on kind.
3. Canonical values fixed per kind in a table: skill (frontmatter fields + body), prompt-section (name/order/complete + static text, or `null` for a per-assembly provider), tool (the `ctx.tools.schemas(agent)` projection), preset (id/trust + include-resolved rows with preset-relative names), plugin (package name + version + `patchLayerSha256`), dynamic-package, agent-provider.
4. `digestBasis: 'content' | 'registration'` on every descriptor — a provider-evaluated prompt section addresses its registration, not the bytes the model saw; rendered bytes stay in `request/header`.
5. Excluded from every digest: viewing scope, cwd, timestamps, absolute paths, discovery `source`/`rank`, provider name, any per-assembly value.
6. `ComponentRegistry` moves from a flat `Map` to `ScopedLayers` (as `ctx.tools`/`ctx.skills` already are), yielding `list({ kind, scope })` and a derived `layer: 'global' | 'agent'`.
7. `composition/manifest` is a log-only `SessionEventMap` member, **required-on-read** (not `ignorable`) because every consumer keys a refusal on it, and carries **no `@mode`** — `gen-persistence-catalog` rejects the tag on log events; the `@mode`/`@param` rules govern the new Cordis event instead.
8. Payload: `kind`, `version: 1`, `reason`, `presetId?`, `components[] {id, digest, kind, provenance, lineage?, layer, digestBasis}`, `compositionSha256`, `dynamicPackagesMounted`, `synthesized[]`. The sketch's `seq` is dropped — the envelope carries it.
9. Writer: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-components-manifest` (`packages/components/components-manifest/`), injecting only `agents` + `components`; on `agent/pre-step` it recomputes and appends only when `compositionSha256` differs — recomputation is what keeps it correct under HMR, late preset mounts, and scope shadowing.
10. Change detection: existing `tools/change`, `system-prompt/change`, `tools/result`, `agent-preset/selected`, `subagent/provider-added|removed` carry the adapters; the one gap is the dynamic Cordis runner, so `dsh-cordis-host-runner` gains `cordis/dynamic-changed(agent, pluginId)` (`@mode emit`, unfiltered).
11. A skill is in play once loaded, not once listed: `skillDigest()` in `dsh-skill`, a `digest` on the `skill` tool's canonical value and on `SkillInvocationSource`, never re-parsing the rendered `<skill_content>` block.
12. Quarantine = `dynamicPackagesMounted`, non-empty `synthesized`, **or no manifest at all**; the scorekeeper invariant rejects a `skill` tool result whose digest no preceding manifest names; `dsh-trajectories` gains `includeQuarantined` + a `quarantined` count and refuses those sessions by default.
13. Ledger: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-archive` (`packages/improvement/archive/`) over `ctx.storage.domain`, tables `variants` (`HarnessVariant`) and `generations` (`id@digest`), statuses `alive`/`dominated`/`promoted`/`deprecated` defined, lineage stored on both ends, mutations mint rows rather than rewrite them.
14. The manifest-versus-ledger invariant lives in `dsh-archive`'s `./invariant`: every `evidenceSessions` entry must carry a manifest occurrence of that exact `id@digest`.
15. Rollout in 7 slices, each green: registry digest+layering → composition-time adapters → manifest writer + event → skill generations → dynamic packages → quarantine consumers → archive ledger.
